ECV is offered from 36–37 weeks in settings with facilities for emergency caesarean section. Options A, C and D are favourable for success and safety. Anti-D should be given to Rh-negative women after the procedure.

questions.q: Which vaccines are given to a healthy newborn at birth under the Kenya Expanded Programme on Immunization?
options: BCG and oral polio vaccine (OPV 0)
Measles and yellow fever
Pentavalent and pneumococcal vaccine
Rotavirus and HPV
questions.explanation: BCG (given intradermally in the right upper arm) and OPV 0 are given at birth, or at the first contact within the first 2 weeks. Pentavalent, pneumococcal and rotavirus vaccines start at 6 weeks, and measles-rubella and yellow fever come later in infancy. HPV is for adolescent girls. Check the current MoH schedule, as it is updated from time to time.

questions.q: After a vaginal delivery, the midwife finds a perineal tear involving the perineal muscles and less than half the thickness of the external anal sphincter. How should this be classified and managed?
options: First-degree tear; no suturing needed
Second-degree tear; repair on the ward
Third-degree (3a) tear; repair by a skilled clinician in theatre with adequate analgesia, with antibiotics
Fourth-degree tear; leave to heal
questions.explanation: A third-degree tear involves the anal sphincter complex. It is graded 3a (less than 50% of the external sphincter), 3b (more than 50%) and 3c (internal sphincter also torn). A fourth-degree tear involves the anal mucosa as well. Repair needs good light, analgesia or anaesthesia, and an experienced operator, because poor repair causes faecal incontinence. A single dose of prophylactic antibiotic, stool softeners and follow-up are recommended. Second-degree tears (B) involve perineal muscles but not the anal sphincter. First-degree tears (A) involve skin only.

questions.q: A breastfeeding mother on day 10 has a painful, red, wedge-shaped area on one breast with a temperature of 38.4°C. The baby is feeding well. What is the best management?
options: Stop breastfeeding from that breast and bind the breast tightly
Continue breastfeeding or expressing from the affected breast, give analgesia, offer rest and fluids
Wean the baby completely
Apply hot compresses and massage the lump firmly
questions.explanation: Mastitis is managed by effective, frequent milk removal, because stasis worsens inflammation. The milk is safe for the baby. Give analgesia, ensure good attachment, and use antibiotics when there is fever with systemic symptoms, a nipple fissure or no improvement in 12–24 hours. Stopping breastfeeding (A, C) increases the risk of abscess. Firm massage (D) can worsen tissue damage. Refer if an abscess forms.

questions.q: Which findings in a pregnant woman are danger signs requiring urgent referral or evaluation? Which combination is correct?
options: A, B, C, E
A, B, C, D, E, F
A, B, C, E, F
D, G
questions.explanation: Correct combination: A, B, C, E, F. Severe headache and visual disturbance suggest severe pre-eclampsia. Bleeding may be placenta praevia, abruption or other causes. Reduced fetal movements may indicate fetal compromise. Preterm rupture of membranes and fever signal infection or preterm labour risk. Heartburn (D) and mild backache (G) are common minor discomforts managed with advice. Other danger signs include convulsions, severe abdominal pain, difficulty breathing and swelling of the face and hands. Teach every woman these signs at each ANC contact. Key: A = Severe headache with blurred vision; B = Vaginal bleeding; C = Reduced or absent fetal movements; D = Mild heartburn after meals; E = Leaking of fluid before 37 weeks; F = Fever with chills; G = Mild backache without other symptoms

questions.q: A mother is starting DMPA-IM injectable contraception. Which counselling is correct?
options: It is given every 3 months (13 weeks), may cause irregular bleeding or amenorrhoea
It is given every 6 months, causes regular periods and protects against STIs
It must be given on day 1 of the period only
It causes permanent infertility
questions.explanation: DMPA-IM 150 mg is given deep IM every 13 weeks (3 months), and the next dose can be given up to 4 weeks late. Common effects are spotting, irregular bleeding and then amenorrhoea, which are not harmful. Return of fertility may be delayed by several months, but it is not permanent. It can be started on any day if pregnancy is reasonably excluded. Advise condom use for STI and HIV protection, and counsel about possible weight gain and bone density concerns with long-term use.

questions.q: At 26 weeks, a woman has a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test with a fasting plasma glucose of 5.3 mmol/L. Using the WHO diagnostic criteria, what is the best interpretation and first step?
options: Normal result; repeat at 36 weeks
Gestational diabetes mellitus; start dietary counselling, physical activity and glucose monitoring
Type 1 diabetes; start insulin immediately
Impaired renal threshold; no action needed
questions.explanation: WHO (2013) diagnoses gestational diabetes at a fasting glucose of 5.1–6.9 mmol/L, a 1-hour value of 10.0 mmol/L or more, or a 2-hour value of 8.5–11.0 mmol/L. A fasting value of 5.3 meets the criterion. First-line management is nutrition counselling, regular activity and self-monitoring, with insulin (or metformin where policy allows) if targets are not met. Fasting plasma glucose of 7.0 mmol/L or more would indicate diabetes in pregnancy. Plan for the baby too, including early feeding and glucose monitoring after birth, and arrange postpartum glucose testing.

questions.q: A newborn has been receiving effective bag-and-mask ventilation with visible chest rise for 30 seconds, and the heart rate is 50/min. What is the next step?
options: Continue ventilation only for another 5 minutes
Start chest compressions at a 3:1 compression-to-ventilation ratio
Give a sodium bicarbonate bolus
Stop resuscitation
questions.explanation: If the heart rate stays below 60/min after 30 seconds of effective ventilation, start chest compressions (two-thumb technique over the lower third of the sternum, to a depth of about one third of the chest) at a ratio of 3 compressions to 1 breath, and use 100% oxygen. Reassess the heart rate every 60 seconds. If it remains below 60 despite effective compressions and ventilation, give IV adrenaline and consider a volume expander. Bicarbonate (C) is not a routine step. Stopping (D) is a decision made by the team based on local protocol after prolonged resuscitation without response.

questions.q: In a vertex delivery, the fetal head has descended, flexed and rotated internally to the occipito-anterior position. Which cardinal movement comes next?
options: Restitution
Flexion
Engagement
Extension
questions.explanation: The order is engagement, descent, flexion, internal rotation, extension, restitution, external rotation and expulsion. After internal rotation, the occiput fits under the symphysis pubis and the head extends to deliver the vertex, brow, face and chin. Restitution (A) follows after the head is born. Engagement (C) and flexion (B) happen earlier.

questions.q: On day 7 postpartum, a woman has pinkish-brown, watery vaginal discharge with no odour and no fever. How should this lochia be described?
options: Lochia rubra
Lochia alba
Lochia serosa
Menstrual flow
questions.explanation: Lochia rubra is red and lasts about 3–4 days. Lochia serosa is pink to brown and watery, lasting from about day 4 to day 10. Lochia alba is yellowish-white and may last up to 2–6 weeks. A return of bright red bleeding, foul smell, fever or large clots is abnormal and needs assessment for retained products or infection. Menses (D) does not return this early in most women, especially if breastfeeding.

questions.q: A woman at 34 weeks has a BP of 170/115 mmHg on two readings 15 minutes apart. She is alert and has no seizures. Which antihypertensive is appropriate for immediate use?
options: Oral nifedipine (immediate-release, 10 mg)
Oral enalapril
Sublingual nifedipine
IV furosemide
questions.explanation: Immediate-release nifedipine 10 mg swallowed is a first-line option for severe hypertension in pregnancy, with BP rechecked after 30 minutes and the dose repeated if needed. The alternatives are IV labetalol and IV hydralazine. ACE inhibitors such as enalapril (B) are contraindicated in pregnancy because of fetal renal toxicity. Sublingual nifedipine (C) can drop BP too sharply and reduce placental perfusion. Furosemide (D) does not treat the hypertension and can reduce plasma volume in pre-eclampsia. Give magnesium sulphate in parallel if the criteria for severe pre-eclampsia are met.

questions.q: A woman at her first ANC visit has a positive syphilis rapid test and no history of treatment. Which drug is recommended for early syphilis in pregnancy?
options: Doxycycline
Ciprofloxacin
Gentamicin
Benzathine penicillin
questions.explanation: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million IU IM is the only reliably effective treatment that also treats the fetus. It is given as a single dose for early syphilis, or as three weekly doses for late or unknown duration. Doxycycline (A) is contraindicated in pregnancy. Ciprofloxacin (B) and gentamicin (C) do not treat syphilis effectively or protect the baby. Treat the partner, counsel on condom use, offer an HIV test, and follow up the newborn. A penicillin-allergic woman needs desensitisation and referral.

questions.q: On the CTG, abrupt decelerations that vary in shape, depth and timing appear with contractions. Which is the most likely cause?
options: Fetal head compression
Uteroplacental insufficiency
Umbilical cord compression
Maternal hypoglycaemia
questions.explanation: Variable decelerations are caused by cord compression. First, change the mother's position (left or right lateral, whichever relieves the pattern), and do a vaginal examination to exclude cord prolapse. If the membranes are ruptured with low fluid, amnioinfusion may help. Persistent severe variables with loss of variability need escalation. Early decelerations mirror contractions and are caused by head compression (A). Late decelerations suggest uteroplacental insufficiency (B).

questions.q: After a delivery, the midwife sees a round, red mass protruding from the vagina and the mother is shocked and in severe pain. The uterine fundus cannot be palpated abdominally. Which is the most appropriate definitive action?
options: Replace the uterus manually
Pull on the cord
Give ergometrine
Massage the fundus
questions.explanation: This is acute uterine inversion. Call for help, treat shock with IV fluids, stop any oxytocin until the uterus is replaced, and replace it promptly by pushing the fundus up through the cervix with the palm of the hand. Leave the placenta in place until the uterus is back in position, because removing it can worsen bleeding. Once replaced, give oxytocin and keep the hand in the uterus until it contracts. Cord traction (B) is a common cause of inversion. Uterotonics before replacement (C) tighten the cervical ring and make replacement harder, and massage (D) cannot correct an inverted fundus.

questions.q: In an area where dietary calcium intake is low, which calcium regimen does WHO recommend to reduce the risk of pre-eclampsia?
options: 250 mg daily from 12 weeks
3 g daily from 28 weeks
1.5–2 g elemental calcium daily from 20 weeks
Calcium only after pre-eclampsia is diagnosed
questions.explanation: WHO recommends 1.5–2.0 g of elemental calcium daily, usually in divided doses, starting from about 20 weeks in populations with low dietary calcium. It should be taken separately from iron, because calcium reduces iron absorption. The doses in A and B are not the evidence-based range. Option D misses the preventive purpose. Low-dose aspirin can also be considered for women at high risk, per national guidance.

questions.q: In the WHO Labour Care Guide, at what duration of pushing in a nulliparous woman does the second stage become longer than usual and prompt a review?
options: 1 hour
3 hours
4 hours
5 hours
questions.explanation: The Labour Care Guide flags pushing of 3 hours or more in nulliparous women (2 hours or more in multiparous women) as longer than usual. The flag calls for assessment of the mother and fetus, position, hydration, bladder, effectiveness of pushing, and a decision about assistance. It is not an automatic indication for instrumental or caesarean delivery. One hour (A) is well within normal. Options C and D are too long to wait before reviewing.

questions.q: Which signs indicate that the placenta has separated from the uterine wall? Which combination is correct?
options: A, B
A, B, C, D
A, B, C
D, E, F
questions.explanation: Correct combination: A, B, C. Classic signs of separation are a gush of blood, a lengthening cord and a firm, globular uterus that rises as the placenta drops into the lower segment. A soft, flat uterus (D) fits an unseparated placenta or atony. If the cord retracts when suprapubic pressure is applied (E), the placenta is still attached (Küstner's sign). Severe pain with shock (F) suggests uterine inversion or rupture, not separation. Key: A = A gush of blood from the vagina; B = Lengthening of the umbilical cord at the introitus; C = The uterus becomes firm and globular and rises in the abdomen; D = The uterus becomes soft and flat; E = The cord retracts into the vagina when suprapubic pressure is applied; F = Severe pain with maternal shock

questions.q: For how long can a copper IUD (TCu380A) provide effective contraception?
options: 3 years
5 years
Lifelong
At least 10 years
questions.explanation: The TCu380A is effective for at least 10 years and may work up to 12 years, and it can be removed at any time with a prompt return to fertility. It does not contain hormones, so it is suitable for breastfeeding women. Advise the woman about possible heavier or longer periods and cramping, and about the need to return for follow-up and for signs of PID or expulsion. It does not protect against STIs. It is not lifelong (C).

questions.q: A newborn is born to a mother who tests HBsAg positive. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Delay the hepatitis B vaccine until 6 weeks
Isolate the baby from the mother
Give the birth-dose hepatitis B vaccine plus HBIG if available
Stop breastfeeding
questions.explanation: Babies of HBsAg-positive mothers should get the first hepatitis B vaccine dose within 24 hours of birth, ideally with hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG) at a different site. They should then complete the full vaccine series and have follow-up testing. Delaying the vaccine to the routine 6-week pentavalent schedule (A) leaves the baby unprotected during the highest-risk period. Breastfeeding (D) is safe, and separation (B) is unnecessary and harms bonding.

questions.q: At 30 weeks, a pregnant woman has a haemoglobin of 8.5 g/dL. According to WHO classification, how should this be graded?
options: Mild anaemia
Moderate anaemia
Severe anaemia
Normal for pregnancy
questions.explanation: In pregnancy, anaemia is defined as Hb below 11 g/dL. It is graded mild at 10.0–10.9, moderate at 7.0–9.9 and severe below 7.0 g/dL. Treat moderate anaemia with daily oral iron (about 120 mg elemental) and folic acid 400 mcg until the Hb normalises, then continue the usual supplementation. Look for causes such as malaria, hookworm and poor diet, and deworm after the first trimester. Severe anaemia, or moderate anaemia near term with symptoms, needs referral and consideration of transfusion.

questions.q: The nurse-midwife is caring for four postnatal women. Which one should be assessed first?
options: A woman 2 hours after delivery with pulse 118/min, BP 90/55 mmHg and a soft fundus
A woman on day 1 with BP 118/76 mmHg, moderate lochia and a firm fundus
A woman on day 3 with bilateral breast engorgement and no fever
A woman on day 2 with perineal pain rated 4/10, voiding normally
questions.explanation: A rising pulse, falling BP and a soft fundus in the first hours after birth point to postpartum haemorrhage with early shock, which is the most time-critical problem. Act immediately: call for help, rub up the fundus, give uterotonics, secure IV access and monitor blood loss. The other three women are stable (B), or have common, manageable issues (C, D), and can be seen afterwards.

questions.q: A woman at 10 weeks' gestation has heavy vaginal bleeding and cramping. The cervical os is open, tissue is felt in the cervical canal, and the uterus is smaller than dates. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Incomplete miscarriage
Threatened miscarriage
Missed miscarriage
Complete miscarriage
questions.explanation: An open os with partly expelled products of conception defines an incomplete miscarriage. Resuscitate if she is bleeding heavily, then empty the uterus by manual vacuum aspiration or medically, for example with misoprostol 600 mcg orally or 400 mcg sublingually in a stable woman under 12 weeks. A threatened miscarriage (B) has a closed os. In a missed miscarriage (C) the embryo has died but there is usually little or no bleeding and a closed os. In a complete miscarriage (D) the products have all been expelled, the os is closed or closing and bleeding has settled.

questions.q: At 12 weeks, a woman has vaginal bleeding, severe vomiting, and a uterus larger than expected for dates. Which additional finding would most strongly support a complete hydatidiform mole?
options: Fetal heart sounds heard with a Pinard stethoscope
A very low serum hCG level
Passage of grape-like vesicles with a "snowstorm" ultrasound appearance
Painful bleeding with a hard, tender uterus
questions.explanation: A molar pregnancy classically shows a uterus larger than dates, markedly raised hCG, hyperemesis, early-onset hypertension and a snowstorm pattern on ultrasound, with no fetus. Management is suction evacuation, followed by serial hCG monitoring for 6–12 months to detect persistent trophoblastic disease. The woman should avoid pregnancy during follow-up and use reliable contraception. Fetal heart sounds (A) would be absent. In a mole the hCG is very high, not low (B). Painful bleeding with a rigid uterus (D) points to abruption, which is a different condition.

questions.q: Which instruction on umbilical cord care is consistent with WHO guidance for a baby born in a clean facility?
options: Apply methylated spirit after every nappy change
Keep the stump clean and dry
Bind the stump firmly with a cord binder
Dust the stump with antibiotic powder daily
questions.explanation: For babies born in a hospital or clinic, WHO recommends clean, dry cord care, with hand washing before handling and no harmful substances applied. Fold nappies below the stump to keep it out of urine and stool. Where home births are common and neonatal mortality is high, daily chlorhexidine application may be recommended under national policy. Spirit (A), binders (C) and powders (D) delay separation and can increase the risk of omphalitis. Teach the mother to return if the skin around the cord is red or the stump has pus.

questions.q: The first twin has just been delivered vaginally. What is the most appropriate next action?
options: Give oxytocin 10 IU IM to the mother immediately
Rupture the second sac straight away and encourage pushing
Cut the cord and discharge the first baby to the nursery without further steps
Clamp the cord, then check the lie, presentation and fetal heart of the second twin by abdominal
questions.explanation: After the first twin is born, clamp and cut the cord, then determine the lie and presentation of the second twin and listen to its heart rate. If the lie is longitudinal and contractions are weak, an oxytocin infusion may be used, and the membranes are ruptured once the presenting part is engaged. Giving oxytocin IM before the second baby is born (A) can cause strong contractions that compromise it, so the uterotonic for AMTSL is given only after the last baby. Rupturing the sac before assessing (B) risks cord prolapse in an unstable lie. Ignoring the second twin (C) is unsafe, as the second twin has a higher risk of hypoxia and malpresentation.

questions.q: On day 5 postpartum, a woman is agitated, believes the baby is "not hers," hears voices telling her to harm the baby, and sleeps very little. What is the priority nursing action?
options: Reassure her that this is common postpartum blues
Stay with her, keep the baby safe with supervised contact only
Give a sedative and plan discharge in the morning
Leave her alone with the baby to promote bonding
questions.explanation: Hallucinations, delusions, agitation and thoughts of harming the baby are features of postpartum psychosis, which is a psychiatric emergency. It usually starts within the first 2 weeks. The priority is the safety of mother and infant, followed by urgent specialist assessment, usually with admission. Blues (A) is mild and resolves without psychotic features. Sedation and early discharge (C) leave the risk unaddressed, and unsupervised contact (D) is dangerous.

questions.q: Which set of conditions must be met for the lactational amenorrhoea method (LAM) to be an effective contraceptive?
options: Baby under 6 months, fully breastfed on demand, and menses not yet returned
Baby under 12 months, any breastfeeding, and menses returned
Baby under 6 months, mixed feeding, and menses not yet returned
Baby over 6 months, exclusive breastfeeding, and menses not yet returned
questions.explanation: LAM gives about 98–99% protection when all three conditions apply: the baby is under 6 months, breastfeeding is exclusive or near exclusive including at night, and the mother has not had a return of menses. Once any condition fails, she needs another method, ideally started before LAM ends. Mixed feeding (C), a returned period (B) or an older baby (D) lowers protection. LAM does not protect against STIs or HIV.

questions.q: During a vaginal breech delivery, the baby's body has been born as far as the umbilicus. What is the correct approach?
options: Pull gently on both legs to speed up delivery
Apply firm fundal pressure with each contraction
Wrap the baby tightly and wait for the next contraction
Support the body without traction, let the arms and head deliver spontaneously
questions.explanation: The principle is "hands off the breech." Traction can extend the arms and the head and lead to entrapment. If the arms do not deliver, use the Løvset manoeuvre. For the head, keep the baby's back anterior and use the Mauriceau–Smellie–Veit manoeuvre or forceps, with flexion of the head maintained. Pulling on the legs (A) and fundal pressure (B) both increase the risk of deflexed head and arm entrapment. Wrapping the baby (C) does not help and traps heat and time. The birth should be attended by a skilled provider, with an obstetrician and neonatal resuscitation equipment ready.

questions.q: According to the WHO Labour Care Guide, how often should cervical dilatation be assessed in the active first stage of labour when there are no complications?
options: Every hour
Every 2 hours
Every 4 hours
Every 8 hours
questions.explanation: WHO (2018) recommends vaginal examination every 4 hours in the active first stage of low-risk labour, unless there is a clinical indication to examine earlier. More frequent examinations add infection risk and discomfort without improving outcomes. Fetal heart rate and contractions are checked more often, typically every 30 minutes, with maternal pulse every 30 minutes and blood pressure and temperature every 4 hours. Intervals of 1 or 2 hours (A, B) are outdated, and 8 hours (D) is too long.

questions.q: The nurse-midwife is looking after four women in labour. Which woman should be seen first?
options: A primigravida at 5 cm, FHR 140/min, coping well
A multigravida at 8 cm, thick meconium-stained liquor and FHR 100/min
A woman at 6 cm who asks for pain relief
A woman at 3 cm with intact membranes and mild contractions
questions.explanation: A baseline fetal heart rate below 110/min with thick meconium suggests fetal compromise and possible hypoxia, and the woman is close to full dilatation. She needs immediate assessment, repositioning, hydration, a check for cord prolapse, and preparation for rapid delivery and neonatal resuscitation, with escalation to the obstetrician. The other women are stable or have non-urgent needs (A, C, D) and can wait a few minutes.

questions.q: What is the recommended dose of tranexamic acid for a woman with postpartum haemorrhage?
options: 1 g IV over 10 minutes, repeated once after 30 minutes if bleeding continues
500 mg IV stat only
2 g IV push over 1 minute
1 g orally every 8 hours
questions.explanation: WHO recommends tranexamic acid 1 g IV (about 1 mL per minute), given as soon as possible and within 3 hours of birth, in addition to standard care. A second 1 g dose is given if bleeding continues after 30 minutes or restarts within 24 hours. It is part of the PPH bundle along with uterine massage, uterotonics, IV fluids and examination for the cause. A faster push (C) can cause hypotension, a lower dose (B) is not evidence-based and oral dosing (D) is too slow to act.

questions.q: A woman at 28 weeks has BP readings of 150/95 mmHg on two occasions 4 hours apart. Her BP was normal at booking at 12 weeks, her urine protein is negative, and she has no symptoms. How should this be classified?
options: Chronic hypertension
Pre-eclampsia with severe features
Gestational hypertension
Eclampsia
questions.explanation: New hypertension (140/90 mmHg or above) after 20 weeks without proteinuria or other organ involvement is gestational hypertension. Monitor BP, urine protein, symptoms, fetal growth and fetal movements, and teach danger signs. About a quarter of cases progress to pre-eclampsia. Chronic hypertension (A) is present before 20 weeks. Severe features (B) would include BP of 160/110 or above, headache, visual disturbance, epigastric pain or abnormal labs. Eclampsia (D) requires a seizure.

questions.q: A woman's last menstrual period began on 10 March 2026. Using Naegele's rule, what is her expected date of delivery?
options: 3 December 2026
10 December 2026
24 December 2026
17 December 2026
questions.explanation: Naegele's rule: add 7 days to the first day of the LMP, subtract 3 months (or add 9 months), and adjust the year. For 10 March 2026, add 7 days to get 17 March, then add 9 months to reach 17 December 2026. The rule assumes a regular 28-day cycle with ovulation on day 14. Early ultrasound dating is more accurate when the LMP is unknown or cycles are irregular.

questions.q: Which factors increase the risk of early-onset neonatal sepsis? Which combination is correct?
options: A, B, C
A, B, C, D, E
A, B, C, D
E, F
questions.explanation: Correct combination: A, B, C, D. Prolonged rupture of membranes, maternal fever or chorioamnionitis, foul-smelling liquor, prematurity, maternal GBS colonisation and repeated vaginal examinations all raise the risk of early-onset sepsis. A term elective caesarean with intact membranes (E) carries a low risk of ascending infection. Exclusive breastfeeding (F) protects the baby. Early signs are poor feeding, lethargy, temperature instability, fast breathing and apnoea, and these call for prompt antibiotics (ampicillin and gentamicin) and referral. Key: A = Rupture of membranes more than 18 hours before birth; B = Maternal fever in labour; C = Foul-smelling liquor; D = Preterm birth; E = Elective caesarean section at term with intact membranes; F = Exclusive breastfeeding

questions.q: Which respiratory rate is normal for a healthy, term newborn at rest?
options: 20–30 breaths per minute
30–40 breaths per minute
40–60 breaths per minute
70–80 breaths per minute
questions.explanation: The normal newborn respiratory rate is 40–60/min, and it may be slightly irregular with brief pauses. Under IMNCI, a rate of 60/min or more in a baby under 2 months is fast breathing and needs assessment for pneumonia or sepsis. Severe chest indrawing, grunting, nasal flaring and cyanosis are danger signs. Rates of 20–40 (A, B) are too slow for a newborn, and 70–80 (D) is fast breathing.

questions.q: A woman with eclampsia has received the magnesium sulphate loading dose. Twenty minutes later she has another convulsion. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Give an additional 2 g magnesium sulphate IV slowly over 5 minutes
Repeat the full 10 g IM dose
Give 4 g IV over 1 minute
Stop magnesium sulphate and switch to diazepam
questions.explanation: If convulsions recur after the loading dose, WHO recommends an extra 2 g of magnesium sulphate IV given slowly over about 5 minutes, after checking for toxicity (reflexes, respiratory rate, urine output). Repeating the full IM dose (B) or pushing 4 g quickly (C) risks toxicity and respiratory arrest. Diazepam (D) is used only when magnesium sulphate is unavailable. Continue to protect the airway, monitor closely, control severe hypertension and plan delivery once she is stable.

questions.q: Under the Kenya Expanded Programme on Immunization, at what ages are the three doses of pentavalent vaccine given?
options: 6, 12 and 18 weeks
2, 4 and 6 weeks
9, 12 and 15 months
6, 10 and 14 weeks
questions.explanation: Pentavalent (DPT-HepB-Hib) is given at 6, 10 and 14 weeks, together with OPV, pneumococcal vaccine and rotavirus as scheduled. The minimum interval between doses is 4 weeks. A late dose is given at the next contact without restarting the series. Intervals in options A, B and C do not match the national schedule. Check the current MoH schedule, as it is updated periodically.

questions.q: One hour after delivery, a woman has continuous bright red bleeding. The fundus is firm and well contracted at the level of the umbilicus. What is the most likely cause?
options: Uterine atony
Genital tract trauma
Retained placental tissue
Coagulopathy
questions.explanation: Continuous bright red bleeding with a firm, contracted uterus suggests a cervical, vaginal or perineal tear, so inspect the genital tract under good light and repair the injury. A soft, boggy uterus would point to atony (A). Retained tissue (C) usually keeps the uterus soft and may cause intermittent bleeding. Coagulopathy (D) shows as blood that does not clot, with oozing from other sites. The four causes of PPH are tone, trauma, tissue and thrombin.

questions.q: For how long is a levonorgestrel two-rod implant (Jadelle) approved to provide contraception?
options: 1 year
3 years
5 years
10 years
questions.explanation: Jadelle is approved for 5 years, and some studies suggest effectiveness may extend further. The woman can have it removed at any time with prompt return of fertility. Counsel on irregular bleeding or amenorrhoea, which are common and not harmful, and on the need to use condoms for STI protection. A single-rod etonogestrel implant has a shorter labelled duration, so check the product. The 10-year option (D) belongs to the copper IUD.

questions.q: A woman arrives in advanced labour with unknown HIV status and no records. Which plan is most appropriate?
options: Offer a rapid HIV test promptly
Wait until after delivery before any testing
Assume she is negative since she has no symptoms
Give infant nevirapine only if the baby appears sick
questions.explanation: Women of unknown status in labour should be offered a rapid test with consent and counselling, without delaying care. A positive result is followed by ART initiation, safe delivery practices, infant prophylaxis from birth, infant feeding counselling and early infant diagnosis. If the test cannot be done, follow the national protocol for the infant, usually exposure prophylaxis. Waiting (B), assuming a negative status (C) and relying on symptoms (D) all miss the window for preventing transmission.

questions.q: Which actions are appropriate in the management of shoulder dystocia? Which combination is correct?
options: A, B, D
A, B, C, D, F
A, B, D, F
C, E
questions.explanation: Correct combination: A, B, D, F. First-line steps are calling for help, McRoberts positioning and suprapubic pressure. Second-line steps are internal manoeuvres (delivering the posterior arm, or rotating the shoulders using Rubin or Woods screw manoeuvres) and the all-fours position. Fundal pressure (C) pushes the anterior shoulder further against the symphysis. Forceful or repeated traction (E) risks brachial plexus injury. Document the time of head delivery and the manoeuvres used, and check the baby for injury and the mother for PPH and tears. Key: A = McRoberts manoeuvre; B = Suprapubic pressure; C = Fundal pressure; D = Delivery of the posterior arm; E = Repeated forceful downward traction on the head; F = Moving the mother onto all fours

questions.q: A newborn weighs 1,800 g at birth. How is this classified?
options: Normal birth weight
Extremely low birth weight
Very low birth weight
Low birth weight
questions.explanation: Low birth weight is below 2,500 g. Very low birth weight is below 1,500 g, and extremely low birth weight is below 1,000 g. A baby of 1,800 g is low birth weight, and should be kept warm with skin-to-skin contact (KMC), fed early with breast milk and monitored for hypoglycaemia, hypothermia and infection. Babies who cannot suck can be fed expressed milk by cup or tube.

questions.q: Which finding best distinguishes true labour from false labour?
options: Contractions that stop when the woman walks about
Contractions that become longer, stronger
Pain felt only in the lower abdomen with no tightening
Irregular contractions that ease with a warm drink
questions.explanation: True labour produces regular contractions that get progressively stronger and more frequent, with effacement and dilatation of the cervix, and often a show. False labour (Braxton Hicks) is irregular, does not intensify and usually eases with rest, hydration or a change of position, without cervical change. Do not label a woman as "not in labour" without a cervical assessment if there are other concerns such as a reduction in fetal movement or ruptured membranes.

questions.q: By about which postpartum day is the uterus no longer palpable abdominally in a normal puerperium?
options: Days 10–14
Days 2–3
Week 6
Month 3
questions.explanation: The uterine fundus descends about 1 cm per day after birth and normally cannot be felt above the symphysis by about 10–14 days. It returns to its pre-pregnancy size by about 6 weeks (C). Delayed involution (subinvolution) suggests retained products, infection or fibroids and should prompt assessment, especially if lochia is heavy, offensive, or accompanied by fever.

questions.q: The nurse reviews four newborns in the postnatal ward. Which baby needs urgent intervention first?
options: A day-4 baby with mild jaundice on the face, feeding well
A baby with milia (small white spots) on the nose
A 2-hour-old baby with grunting, nasal flaring, chest indrawing
A baby with acrocyanosis of the hands and feet only
questions.explanation: Grunting, nasal flaring, retractions and fast breathing indicate respiratory distress. Keep the baby warm, check oxygen saturation, give oxygen if saturation is low, check glucose, evaluate for sepsis, and escalate promptly. The other findings are benign: mild day-4 jaundice in a well baby (A), milia (B) and acrocyanosis in the first hours or days (D).

questions.q: A pregnant woman with no previous tetanus vaccination receives her first Td dose at the booking visit. When should the second dose be given?
options: One week later
During labour
Six months later
At least 4 weeks later
questions.explanation: Two doses at least 4 weeks apart, with the second given at least 2 weeks before delivery, protect the mother and prevent neonatal tetanus. Additional doses (a third at 6 months, then at 1 year and at the next pregnancy) provide lifelong protection, up to 5 doses in total. Doses given too close together (A) or too late (B) do not give adequate protection, and waiting 6 months (C) leaves the baby unprotected at delivery.

questions.q: Which instruction on kangaroo mother care (KMC) is correct?
options: Dress the baby warmly and place her in a cot beside the mother
Place the baby upright, skin-to-skin between the mother's breasts, covered with a cloth, for as many hours a day as possible
Hold the baby skin-to-skin for 10 minutes twice a day
Use KMC only for babies who weigh more than 2,500 g
questions.explanation: KMC involves continuous or near-continuous skin-to-skin contact in an upright position, with a hat and a wrap to keep the baby secure. Breastfeeding is encouraged on demand. It reduces hypothermia, sepsis and mortality in stable low birth weight babies and can be provided by the father or another family member. Short, scheduled sessions (C) give less benefit, a cot alone (A) is not skin-to-skin, and KMC is intended mainly for babies under 2,500 g (D).

questions.q: Which of the following is a positive (definite) sign of pregnancy?
options: Amenorrhoea
Fetal heart sounds heard by the examiner
A positive urine pregnancy test
Chadwick's sign
questions.explanation: Positive signs can only be caused by a fetus. They are fetal heart sounds heard by the examiner, fetal movements felt by the examiner, and visualisation of the fetus on ultrasound. Amenorrhoea (A) is a presumptive sign. A positive urine test (C) and Chadwick's sign, the bluish discolouration of the vagina and cervix (D), are probable signs, because other conditions such as a molar pregnancy or hCG-secreting tumours can mimic them.

questions.q: A 5-hour-old baby of a diabetic mother is jittery and lethargic. The blood glucose is 1.4 mmol/L. What is the best action?
options: Offer a breastfeed and recheck in 3 hours
Give 5 mL of sterile water by cup
Start skin-to-skin contact and observe only
Give 10% dextrose 2 mL/kg IV as a slow bolus, then start a glucose infusion
questions.explanation: A symptomatic baby with a very low glucose needs IV dextrose without delay. The bolus is followed by a maintenance infusion, with frequent monitoring until the glucose is stable. Feeding can continue as soon as the baby is able. Oral feeding alone (A) is for asymptomatic, borderline values. Sterile water (B) provides no calories, and observation only (C) risks seizures and brain injury.

questions.q: A woman at 24 weeks' gestation has a positive malaria test with fever and no signs of severity. Which treatment is recommended?
options: Artemether-lumefantrine for 3 days
A single dose of sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine
Chloroquine for 3 days
Primaquine for 14 days
questions.explanation: In the second and third trimesters, uncomplicated malaria is treated with artemether-lumefantrine (AL) for 3 days, taken with fatty food or milk. In the first trimester, the preferred option is oral quinine plus clindamycin, with AL used if there is no alternative. Sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (B) is for IPTp, not treatment. Chloroquine (C) is no longer effective against most P. falciparum, and primaquine (D) is not used in pregnancy. Severe malaria needs IV artesunate and referral.

questions.q: A woman is having labour induced with an oxytocin infusion. Which finding requires the nurse to stop the infusion?
options: Three contractions in 10 minutes, each lasting about 40 seconds
Cervical dilatation progressing at 1 cm per hour
Six contractions in 10 minutes with late decelerations
A fetal heart rate of 140 bpm with accelerations
questions.explanation: More than five contractions in 10 minutes (uterine tachysystole) with fetal heart rate changes indicates hyperstimulation and risks fetal hypoxia. Stop the infusion, turn the woman to the left side, give IV fluids and oxygen if needed, and notify the doctor. Options A, B and D describe adequate, effective labour with a reassuring fetus. Titrate oxytocin to the lowest dose that achieves effective contractions.

questions.q: Which findings meet the criteria for pre-eclampsia with severe features? Which combination is correct?
options: A, C, D
A, B, C, D, F
A, C, D, F
B, E
questions.explanation: Correct combination: A, C, D, F. Severe features include BP of 160/110 or above, thrombocytopenia (below 100 × 10⁹/L), severe persistent headache or visual symptoms, pulmonary oedema, impaired liver function, renal impairment, and epigastric or right upper quadrant pain. Mild oedema (B) is common in normal pregnancy, and trace proteinuria with normal BP (E) does not meet any criterion. Manage with magnesium sulphate, antihypertensives, close monitoring and delivery planning. Key: A = BP of 165/112 mmHg on two readings; B = Mild ankle swelling with BP of 142/92 mmHg; C = Platelet count of 80 × 10⁹/L; D = Persistent severe headache with visual disturbance; E = Trace proteinuria on dipstick with normal BP; F = Pulmonary oedema

questions.q: On abdominal palpation, the midwife feels a hard, round, ballotable mass at the fundus and a broad, soft mass above the pelvic brim. What is the presentation?
options: Cephalic (vertex)
Breech
Transverse lie
Face
questions.explanation: A firm, round, ballotable head at the fundus with a softer, irregular breech in the lower pole indicates a breech presentation. In a cephalic presentation (A) the head is the hard, round part found at the pelvic brim. In a transverse lie (C) the fundus is empty and the long axis of the fetus lies across the mother's abdomen. Confirm with ultrasound and plan the mode of delivery, offering ECV at 36–37 weeks if there is no contraindication.

questions.q: According to the WHO postnatal care recommendations, when should a healthy mother and baby have routine postnatal contacts?
options: At 24 hours and again at 12 weeks
Day 7, week 4 and week 8 after birth
Only at 6 weeks, unless a problem occurs
At 24 hours, day 3, days 7–14 and week 6
questions.explanation: WHO (2022) recommends at least four postnatal contacts after a facility birth: within 24 hours, on day 3 (48–72 hours), between days 7 and 14, and at 6 weeks. Mothers and babies should stay at least 24 hours in the facility after a vaginal birth. Each contact covers danger signs, bleeding, BP, breastfeeding, newborn assessment, immunisation, mental wellbeing and family planning. Schedules A, B and C leave out the critical early period.

questions.q: Which situation is a contraindication to vacuum-assisted delivery?
options: Gestational age of 32 weeks
Fully dilated cervix
Occipito-anterior position with the head at +2 station
Ruptured membranes
questions.explanation: Vacuum extraction is not advised before 34 weeks (and is used with caution up to 36 weeks), because of the risk of intracranial haemorrhage in the preterm head. Other contraindications include face or brow presentation, breech, an unengaged head, an unknown position, a cervix not fully dilated, and suspected fetal bleeding disorders. A fully dilated cervix (B), a known occipito-anterior position with a low head (C) and ruptured membranes (D) are prerequisites for the procedure.

questions.q: Six hours after delivery, a woman cannot pass urine. A rounded, tender swelling is felt above the symphysis, and the fundus is soft and pushed to one side. What is the best action?
options: Give an additional dose of oxytocin
Restrict her fluids
Help her to pass urine in privacy, run warm water
Massage the fundus vigorously until it moves back to the midline
questions.explanation: A distended bladder displaces the uterus and prevents it from contracting properly, which can cause PPH. Emptying the bladder is the priority. Use non-invasive measures first (privacy, warm water over the perineum, walking to the toilet), and catheterise if these fail. Record the volume drained and monitor voiding afterwards. Oxytocin (A) will not solve the cause, fluid restriction (B) is not appropriate, and vigorous massage (D) is painful and will not shift the displaced uterus.

questions.q: A woman who is positive for group B Streptococcus is in labour at term. Which plan is most appropriate?
options: Oral amoxicillin at the start of labour only
IV benzylpenicillin (or ampicillin) at the onset of labour, then 4-hourly until delivery
A single IM dose at 36 weeks of the pregnancy
Treat the baby only after birth if symptoms appear
questions.explanation: Intrapartum IV antibiotic prophylaxis, started early and continued until delivery, reduces early-onset neonatal GBS sepsis. Penicillin G or ampicillin are first line, and cefazolin or alternatives are used in penicillin allergy according to the severity of the allergy. Prophylaxis is also indicated with previous GBS-infected infants, GBS bacteriuria, preterm labour, ruptured membranes for more than 18 hours, or fever in labour. Oral or antenatal-only treatment (A, C) does not provide reliable levels at birth, and waiting for symptoms (D) delays treatment.

questions.q: What is the correct infant feeding advice for a healthy baby up to 2 years of age?
options: Give breast milk for 4 months, then stop and start family foods
Give breast milk and water from 2 months to prevent thirst
Breastfeed exclusively until 12 months without any other food
Breastfeed exclusively for 6 months, then add complementary foods
questions.explanation: WHO and the Kenya MoH recommend exclusive breastfeeding for the first 6 months (no water, other milks or foods), followed by safe, nutritious complementary foods while breastfeeding continues up to 2 years or beyond. Early weaning (A) and early water (B) increase the risk of diarrhoea and malnutrition, and exclusive milk beyond 6 months (C) cannot meet the baby's iron and energy needs. HIV-positive mothers on ART are usually advised to follow the same schedule under current national guidance.

questions.q: A baby is born through thick meconium-stained liquor. The baby is limp and not breathing after birth. What is the correct action?
options: Dry, stimulate and position the airway, then start bag-and-mask ventilation if breathing remains absent
Perform routine tracheal intubation and suction before stimulating
Perform gastric lavage first
Delay ventilation until all the meconium has been removed
questions.explanation: Current guidance no longer recommends routine tracheal suction for non-vigorous babies born through meconium, because it delays ventilation without improving outcomes. Follow the standard steps: dry, stimulate, clear the airway only if the mouth or nose is visibly blocked, and start positive-pressure ventilation within the first minute if the baby is still not breathing. Intubation and suction are considered only if ventilation is not effective and an obstruction is suspected. Gastric lavage (C) has no role here, and delaying ventilation (D) increases hypoxia.

questions.q: According to WHO, postpartum haemorrhage is defined as blood loss of at least:
options: 200 mL within 1 hour of birth
300 mL within 6 hours of birth
500 mL within 24 hours of birth
2,000 mL within 24 hours of birth
questions.explanation: WHO defines PPH as blood loss of 500 mL or more within 24 hours of birth, and severe PPH as 1,000 mL or more. Any blood loss that causes signs of haemodynamic instability should be treated as PPH, regardless of volume, and measured blood loss is more accurate than visual estimation. Primary PPH occurs within the first 24 hours, and secondary PPH occurs after 24 hours and up to 12 weeks.

questions.q: According to WHO, when should the umbilical cord be clamped in a vigorous term baby who does not need resuscitation?
options: Immediately after the baby is born
Not earlier than 1 minute after birth
After exactly 10 minutes
Only after the placenta is delivered
questions.explanation: WHO recommends delayed cord clamping, not earlier than 1 minute after birth, because it improves infant iron stores and haemoglobin and reduces anaemia in later infancy. Immediate clamping (A) is reserved for situations where the mother or baby needs urgent care. Waiting 10 minutes (C) or until the placenta is out (D) is not recommended practice. If the baby needs resuscitation, start it with the cord intact if possible, or clamp and cut the cord and move the baby to the resuscitation area.

questions.q: Before inducing labour, the midwife assesses the cervix using the Bishop score. Which total score indicates a favourable cervix?
options: 8 or above
questions.explanation: The Bishop score rates dilatation, effacement, station, cervical consistency and position. A score of 8 or above predicts a good chance of successful vaginal delivery after induction. A score of 6 or less suggests the cervix is unfavourable and needs ripening, for example with a prostaglandin or a Foley catheter, before oxytocin is started. A score of 6–7 is borderline.

questions.q: Which regimen is recommended for induction of labour at term with misoprostol in a woman with a live fetus and no uterine scar?
options: 25 mcg vaginally, repeated every 6 hours
200 mcg vaginally every 4 hours
600 mcg sublingually as a single dose
50 mcg orally as a single dose
questions.explanation: Low-dose misoprostol (25 mcg vaginally every 6 hours, or 25 mcg orally every 2 hours) is the WHO-recommended regimen. Higher doses (B, C) cause uterine hyperstimulation, fetal distress and rupture. Misoprostol should not be used in women with a previous caesarean scar. Monitor the contractions and fetal heart rate, and do not give oxytocin until at least 6 hours after the last dose.

questions.q: A woman at 9 weeks has persistent vomiting more than 10 times a day, ketonuria, a 5% weight loss and dry mucous membranes. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Advise dry crackers and sips of water at home
Plan termination of pregnancy
Admit for IV isotonic fluids, thiamine and antiemetics
Discharge with reassurance that this is normal morning sickness
questions.explanation: Hyperemesis gravidarum causes dehydration, ketosis and electrolyte disturbance. Treatment includes IV rehydration (with potassium replaced according to the results), antiemetics such as promethazine or metoclopramide, and thiamine before or with dextrose to prevent Wernicke's encephalopathy. Dietary advice alone (A) and reassurance (D) are inadequate at this severity. Termination (B) is rarely needed. Consider a molar pregnancy or multiple pregnancy, and check for thyroid disease and urinary tract infection.

questions.q: After a vaginal birth, the uterus remains soft despite fundal massage and a uterotonic, and bleeding is heavy. What is the next appropriate action?
options: Wait one more hour before taking action
Perform bimanual uterine compression while preparing for further treatment
Give the woman a warm sitz bath
Apply an abdominal binder only
questions.explanation: Bimanual compression, with one hand in the vagina pressing the anterior uterine wall and the other on the abdomen compressing the posterior wall, controls bleeding from atony while further measures are arranged. These measures include a second-line uterotonic, tranexamic acid, IV fluids, a uterine balloon tamponade and surgery. Delay (A) is dangerous, and a sitz bath (C) or a binder (D) will not control the bleeding.

questions.q: Which findings indicate magnesium sulphate toxicity or a warning that it is accumulating? Which combination is correct?
options: A, B, C
A, B, C, D, E
A, B, C, E
D, F
questions.explanation: Correct combination: A, B, C, E. Magnesium is cleared by the kidneys, so oliguria is a warning that the drug may accumulate. Toxicity progresses from loss of reflexes to drowsiness, slurred speech, respiratory depression and cardiac arrest. Withhold the next dose, and give calcium gluconate 1 g IV slowly if respiratory depression occurs. Brisk reflexes (D) are not a sign of toxicity, and a high BP (F) needs antihypertensive treatment but does not point to magnesium toxicity. Key: A = Loss of patellar reflexes; B = Respiratory rate below 16 breaths per minute; C = Urine output below 30 mL per hour; D = Brisk, easily elicited reflexes; E = Drowsiness with slurred speech; F = BP of 170/110 mmHg

questions.q: A mother who has completed her family wants postpartum tubal ligation by minilaparotomy. When is it generally acceptable to do it?
options: At 2 weeks postpartum
At 3 weeks postpartum
At 4 weeks postpartum
Within 7 days of delivery, or at 6 weeks or later
questions.explanation: Under WHO eligibility guidance, postpartum female sterilisation is acceptable within 7 days of delivery, when the uterus is still large and accessible, or after 6 weeks. Between 7 days and 6 weeks, it is usually delayed. Counselling must be thorough, voluntary and without coercion, since the procedure is intended to be permanent. Explain that it does not protect against STIs or HIV.

questions.q: Which mother-baby blood group combination carries the highest risk of ABO haemolytic disease of the newborn?
options: Mother group O, baby group A or B
Mother group A, baby group O
Mother group AB, baby group O
Mother group B, baby group B
questions.explanation: Group O mothers naturally carry IgG anti-A and anti-B antibodies that cross the placenta and can haemolyse the red cells of an A or B baby. The jaundice usually appears within the first 24–48 hours, and the direct Coombs test may be weakly positive. Mother group A or AB with a group O baby (B, C) has no target antigen on the baby's cells, and a matching group (D) carries no risk. Management includes bilirubin monitoring and phototherapy.

questions.q: Which Leopold manoeuvre is used to identify the part of the fetus presenting at the pelvic brim?
options: The first (fundal) grip
The second (lateral) grip
The third (pelvic or Pawlik) grip
The fourth grip, which is used only to assess the fetal heart
questions.explanation: The first grip identifies the fetal part in the fundus, the second locates the back and limbs, and the third identifies the presenting part and whether it is engaged or mobile. The fourth grip, which faces the mother's feet, assesses the degree of descent and flexion. It is not used for fetal heart assessment (D). Always empty the bladder, explain the procedure and warm the hands before palpation.

questions.q: A woman who is Rh-negative with no antibodies is at 28 weeks. Which plan is correct?
options: Give anti-D only at 12 weeks
Give anti-D at 28 weeks
Give anti-D only if she already has anti-D antibodies
Give anti-D only after delivery of the first baby
questions.explanation: Routine antenatal prophylaxis at about 28 weeks reduces sensitisation caused by silent fetomaternal bleeding, and a postnatal dose follows within 72 hours if the baby is Rh-positive. Anti-D is also given after sensitising events such as bleeding, abdominal trauma, ECV, miscarriage or amniocentesis. If she already has antibodies (C), anti-D is of no use. Giving it only at 12 weeks (A) or only after the first delivery (D) leaves gaps in protection.

questions.q: What is the recommended total weight gain during pregnancy for a woman with a normal pre-pregnancy BMI?
options: 2–4 kg
5–7 kg
About 11–16 kg
questions.explanation: For a woman with a normal BMI, the recommended gain is about 11.5–16 kg. Women who are underweight should gain more, and those who are overweight or obese should gain less. Very low gain is linked to low birth weight and preterm birth, and excessive gain is linked to macrosomia, gestational diabetes and caesarean delivery. In undernourished populations, balanced energy and protein supplementation is recommended.

questions.q: A jaundiced newborn is receiving phototherapy. Which nursing action is correct?
options: Cover the eyes, expose as much skin as possible, continue feeding, and monitor temperature and hydration
Dress the baby in a woollen suit to prevent cold
Restrict feeds to reduce the number of stools
Place the baby one metre from the lamp with the eyes uncovered to avoid pressure on the face
questions.explanation: Eye protection prevents retinal damage, and maximum skin exposure improves effectiveness. Frequent feeds (breast milk if possible) promote bilirubin excretion, and the baby should be turned regularly. Monitor the temperature, hydration, and serum bilirubin as per protocol. Clothing (B) blocks the light, restricting feeds (C) worsens dehydration and jaundice, and leaving the eyes uncovered (D) risks eye injury. Phototherapy is stopped once the bilirubin is safely below the treatment threshold.

questions.q: In the context of labour, what does effacement mean?
options: Descent of the fetal head into the pelvis
Opening of the cervical os
Thinning and shortening of the cervix
Softening of the cervix only
questions.explanation: Effacement is the progressive thinning and shortening of the cervix, expressed as a percentage from 0% (a long cervix of about 3 cm) to 100% (paper-thin). It occurs along with dilatation, which is the widening of the os (B). In a primigravida, effacement generally precedes dilatation, whereas in a multigravida the two often occur together. Descent (A) is measured as station.

questions.q: A pregnant woman at her ANC visit has no urinary symptoms, but a urine culture shows significant bacteriuria. What is the best action?
options: Take no action, as she has no symptoms
Treat only if fever develops
Give a 7-day course of a suitable antibiotic
Give a single dose of paracetamol
questions.explanation: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy should be treated, because it can progress to pyelonephritis and is linked to preterm birth and low birth weight. WHO recommends a 7-day antibiotic course, chosen by culture sensitivity and safety in pregnancy (for example amoxicillin or cefalexin). Waiting for symptoms (A, B) misses the chance to prevent complications, and paracetamol (D) does not treat the infection. Repeat the culture after treatment to confirm clearance.

questions.q: During labour, a woman suddenly becomes breathless, cyanosed and hypotensive, then loses consciousness. Amniotic fluid embolism is suspected. What is the priority action?
options: Call for help, start resuscitation with oxygen
Give an oral antihypertensive
Encourage her to continue pushing
Give ergometrine to contract the uterus
questions.explanation: Amniotic fluid embolism causes abrupt cardiorespiratory collapse, often followed by coagulopathy and haemorrhage. Management is supportive: a multidisciplinary team call, airway and oxygen, CPR if arrest occurs (with manual left uterine displacement), IV access, fluids, blood and clotting products, and expedited delivery if the baby is undelivered and she is in arrest. Oral drugs (B) are unsafe in a collapsed patient, pushing (C) is inappropriate, and ergometrine (D) can worsen the haemodynamic picture.

questions.q: What is the dose and interval for subcutaneous DMPA (DMPA-SC, such as Sayana Press)?
options: 150 mg every month
104 mg every 6 months
150 mg every 8 weeks
104 mg every 3 months
questions.explanation: DMPA-SC contains 104 mg medroxyprogesterone acetate, given subcutaneously every 3 months (13 weeks), and WHO allows the injection to be given up to 4 weeks late without a need for extra protection. It can be self-injected after training. The 150 mg dose is the intramuscular formulation (DMPA-IM), also given every 3 months. Neither product is given monthly or six-monthly. Counsel on menstrual changes and delayed return of fertility, and advise condoms for STI and HIV protection.

questions.q: A baby born at 30 weeks weighs 1,300 g and has an immature suck and swallow. Which feeding plan is most appropriate?
options: Direct breastfeeding on demand from birth
Expressed breast milk by nasogastric tube, with progression to cup
Cow's milk formula by bottle
Glucose water by bottle for the first 3 days
questions.explanation: Very preterm babies often cannot coordinate sucking, swallowing and breathing until about 32–34 weeks. Expressed breast milk is the preferred feed because it lowers the risk of necrotising enterocolitis and infection, and it can be given by nasogastric tube or cup. Skin-to-skin KMC supports lactation and feeding readiness. Attempts at the breast begin as soon as the baby shows cues. Bottles (C, D) and unsupported breastfeeding (A) risk aspiration and exhaustion.

questions.q: Which factors increase the risk of umbilical cord prolapse? Which combination is correct?
options: A, B, C, E
A, B, C, D, E, F
A, B, C, E, F
D
questions.explanation: Correct combination: A, B, C, E, F. Cord prolapse is more likely when the presenting part does not fill the pelvic inlet, so malpresentation, a small preterm fetus, excess liquor, twins and rupture of membranes with a high head all increase the risk. A well-engaged vertex (D) seals the pelvic inlet and lowers the risk. Avoid artificial rupture of membranes with a high head, and perform a vaginal examination after spontaneous rupture when the fetal heart rate changes. Key: A = Breech presentation; B = Polyhydramnios; C = Prematurity; D = A well-engaged vertex with the head well applied to the cervix; E = Multiple pregnancy; F = Artificial rupture of membranes with a high presenting part

questions.q: What is the WHO position on episiotomy?
options: Routine for all first-time mothers
Routine for all women giving birth to a baby over 3 kg
Selective use for clinical indications, not routine use
Routine for all preterm births
questions.explanation: WHO recommends against routine or liberal episiotomy in spontaneous vaginal birth. Restrictive use, for example in fetal distress that requires prompt delivery, or in shoulder dystocia or some instrumental births, results in less severe perineal trauma and fewer complications. If an episiotomy is done, give effective local anaesthesia and repair it promptly with a suitable suture technique. Options A, B and D describe routine use that is not evidence-based.

questions.q: A woman at 36 weeks has a haemoglobin of 6.0 g/dL, with pallor, tachycardia and breathlessness on exertion. What is the best plan?
options: Admit, plan blood transfusion, treat the cause
Give oral iron alone and review in 4 weeks
Give an antimalarial treatment dose only
Reassure her, since this is expected near term
questions.explanation: Severe anaemia near term increases the risk of cardiac failure, preterm birth, and death from even a modest haemorrhage at delivery. Transfuse where she is symptomatic or close to term, give oxygen, and evaluate causes such as malaria, hookworm and nutritional deficiency. Deliver in a facility with blood and skilled staff, with active management of the third stage. Oral iron alone (B) is too slow to correct the Hb before delivery. Dealing with only one cause (C) and reassurance (D) are inadequate.

questions.q: At what times is the Apgar score routinely recorded?
options: At 30 seconds and 2 minutes
At 10 and 20 minutes
At 1 hour and 6 hours
At 1 minute and 5 minutes
questions.explanation: The Apgar score is routinely recorded at 1 and 5 minutes after birth. If the 5-minute score is below 7, it is repeated every 5 minutes for up to 20 minutes. The score describes the baby's condition and the response to resuscitation. It should not be used to decide whether to start resuscitation, which is based on the baby's breathing and heart rate at birth.

questions.q: On day 3, a breastfeeding mother has full, hard, tender breasts with no fever, and the baby is struggling to latch. What is the best advice?
options: Stop breastfeeding for 24 hours to let the breasts rest
Feed frequently, hand express a little milk to soften the areola before feeds, use a cold compress after feeds
Bind both breasts tightly and restrict fluids
Start a milk suppressant and stop feeds
questions.explanation: Engorgement results from milk accumulation and tissue oedema. Frequent, effective milk removal is the key, along with softening the areola so the baby can attach, and cold compresses or analgesia for comfort. Stopping feeds (A, D) and binding (C) increase the risk of mastitis and abscess. If she develops fever, redness or a wedge-shaped painful area, evaluate her for mastitis.

questions.q: What is the normal heart rate of a healthy term newborn?
options: 60–80 beats per minute
80–100 beats per minute
120–160 beats per minute
180–200 beats per minute
questions.explanation: The normal newborn heart rate is 120–160 bpm, and it may fall to about 100 during sleep. A heart rate below 100 in a baby who is not responding needs urgent assessment and support of ventilation, and below 60 despite effective ventilation is an indication for chest compressions. Persistent rates above 160–180 suggest fever, infection, hypovolaemia or an arrhythmia.

questions.q: A woman with severe pre-eclampsia is on the magnesium sulphate maintenance regimen. For how long should it continue after delivery?
options: 24 hours after delivery or after the last convulsion, whichever is later
6 hours after delivery
72 hours after delivery
7 days after delivery
questions.explanation: Maintenance magnesium sulphate, 5 g IM every 4 hours alternating buttocks (or an IV infusion at 1 g/hr), is continued for 24 hours after delivery, or after the last convulsion if that is later. Check reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output before each dose. Shorter courses (B) risk recurrent seizures, while longer courses (C, D) increase toxicity without added benefit. Continue BP control and monitoring after the drug is stopped.

questions.q: A woman gives birth at home attended by a trained health worker, and oxytocin is not available. Which uterotonic is recommended for PPH prevention?
options: Ergometrine 0.5 mg orally
Misoprostol 200 mcg sublingually
Oxytocin 5 IU orally
Misoprostol 600 mcg orally
questions.explanation: Where oxytocin cannot be used, WHO recommends misoprostol 600 mcg orally, given after the birth of the baby once a second fetus is excluded. Side effects include shivering and fever. Misoprostol should not be used for PPH prevention by those who lack training. Oral ergometrine (A) and oral oxytocin (C) are not effective prophylaxis, and 200 mcg (B) is a sub-therapeutic dose for this purpose.

questions.q: In labour at term, a woman has a temperature of 38.5°C, maternal pulse of 120/min, fetal heart rate of 175/min, a tender uterus and foul-smelling liquor. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Give paracetamol and observe for 6 hours
Start broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, plan delivery
Discharge her home with oral antibiotics
Delay delivery until 41 weeks
questions.explanation: These features indicate chorioamnionitis, which is an intrapartum infection that threatens both mother and baby. Start IV antibiotics (such as ampicillin plus gentamicin) without delay, and deliver by the safest route without waiting for a specific time. Chorioamnionitis alone is not an indication for caesarean section. Prepare for neonatal sepsis evaluation and treatment, and give a uterotonic and monitor for PPH, since infection predisposes to atony. Antipyretics alone (A), discharge (C) and delay (D) are unsafe.

questions.q: By how much does a woman's blood volume increase by the third trimester of a normal pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Blood volume rises by about 40–50%, peaking around 32–34 weeks. Plasma volume increases more than red cell mass, so the haemoglobin concentration falls slightly (physiological haemodilution). This adaptation supplies the placenta and helps the woman tolerate blood loss at delivery. Hb below 11 g/dL is still treated as anaemia, so a low value should not be dismissed as physiological.

questions.q: On day 12 postpartum, a woman has sudden heavy bleeding with clots, foul-smelling lochia, a low-grade fever and a soft, bulky uterus. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Secondary PPH from retained tissue with infection
Normal lochia serosa in the second week
Primary PPH due to uterine atony
Early return of menstruation
questions.explanation: Heavy bleeding after 24 hours and up to 12 weeks is secondary PPH, most often from retained placental tissue or membranes and endometritis. Resuscitate and set up IV access, give a uterotonic, start broad-spectrum antibiotics (such as ampicillin, gentamicin and metronidazole), and arrange evacuation of the uterus, usually by a skilled provider with analgesia. Primary PPH (C) occurs within 24 hours. Normal lochia (B) is not heavy or offensive, and menses (D) do not explain the fever and foul discharge.

questions.q: Which newborn eye care is consistent with Kenya's essential newborn care guidance?
options: Gentamicin eye drops 4-hourly for a week
Tetracycline 1% eye ointment to both eyes once, soon after birth
Breast milk dropped into the eyes
Irrigation with sterile water only
questions.explanation: A single application of tetracycline 1% eye ointment after birth is used to prevent ophthalmia neonatorum from gonococcal and chlamydial infection. Practice varies by country, and the best prevention is screening and treating maternal STIs in pregnancy. Prolonged drops (A) are not prophylaxis, and breast milk (C) or water alone (D) do not give reliable protection. A baby with swollen, purulent eyes in the first days needs urgent treatment.

questions.q: Which actions are appropriate for a woman with cord prolapse and a live fetus in the first stage of labour? Which combination is correct?
options: A, B, D
A, B, C, D, F
A, B, D, F
C, E
questions.explanation: Correct combination: A, B, D, F. The aims are to relieve cord compression and deliver quickly. Position change and manual elevation of the presenting part reduce pressure, and moist, warm gauze prevents vasospasm. Handle the cord as little as possible and avoid replacing it (C). Pushing (E) increases compression. Emergency caesarean is the usual route when vaginal delivery is not imminent. Keep the bladder filled via catheter if transfer is needed, as this helps to lift the presenting part. Key: A = Place her in the knee-chest or exaggerated Sims position; B = Manually elevate the presenting part off the cord; C = Push the cord back into the vagina; D = Cover the cord with warm, moist saline gauze; E = Encourage her to push; F = Prepare urgently for caesarean section

questions.q: When is postpartum IUD insertion generally appropriate?
options: Between 3 and 14 days after delivery
Between 7 and 21 days after delivery
At 3 weeks only
Within 48 hours of delivery, or at 4 weeks or later
questions.explanation: The IUD can be inserted within 48 hours of delivery by a trained provider, or from 4 weeks postpartum. Between 48 hours and 4 weeks, the risks of expulsion and perforation are higher, and insertion is generally delayed. It should not be inserted if there is puerperal sepsis or unresolved PPH. Counsel about expulsion, heavier periods, and signs of infection.

questions.q: A 4-day-old jaundiced baby is being assessed. Which finding is most concerning for acute bilirubin encephalopathy?
options: Sneezing and hiccups
Yellow sclerae with good feeding
A high-pitched cry, lethargy
Passing yellow stools
questions.explanation: Lethargy, poor suck, a high-pitched cry, hypertonia and arching (opisthotonos) suggest bilirubin entering the brain, which can lead to kernicterus. This is an emergency requiring urgent bilirubin measurement and intensive phototherapy, with exchange transfusion considered. Sneezing and hiccups (A) are normal newborn behaviours. Jaundice with good feeding (B) and yellow stools (D) are common in healthy, feeding babies.

questions.q: A woman who previously had a baby with a neural tube defect is planning another pregnancy. Which folic acid advice is correct?
options: 0.4 mg daily starting at 12 weeks
4–5 mg daily from before conception until 12 weeks
0.4 mg daily only after the first scan
None, if her diet includes green vegetables
questions.explanation: Women at high risk of neural tube defects (a previous affected pregnancy, or on certain anticonvulsants) are advised a higher dose, 4–5 mg daily, starting at least one month before conception and continuing through the first trimester. The neural tube closes by about 6 weeks, often before pregnancy is recognised, so late or low-dose supplementation (A, C) is not adequate. Diet alone (D) is not enough to prevent recurrence.

questions.q: A woman is fully dilated and feels the urge to push. Which approach to the second stage is consistent with WHO recommendations?
options: Encourage spontaneous bearing down when she feels the urge, in a position she chooses
Instruct sustained breath-holding pushes for 10 seconds, three times each contraction
Start directed pushing as soon as full dilatation is found, even without an urge
Apply fundal pressure to shorten the second stage
questions.explanation: WHO recommends supporting women to push spontaneously, following their own urge, and to choose upright or lateral positions. Prolonged, directed breath-holding does not shorten labour and may reduce fetal oxygenation. Fundal pressure (D) is not recommended and carries a risk of uterine rupture and perineal trauma. Monitor the fetal heart rate and progress, and use the Labour Care Guide flags (3 hours for nulliparous, 2 hours for multiparous women) to prompt review.

questions.q: Which diameter of the fetal skull presents in a well-flexed vertex presentation?
options: Mentovertical, 13.5 cm
Occipitofrontal, 11.5 cm
Submentobregmatic, 9.5 cm
Suboccipitobregmatic, 9.5 cm
questions.explanation: With good flexion, the smallest diameter, the suboccipitobregmatic (about 9.5 cm), presents to the pelvis, which favours easy passage. A deflexed head presents the larger occipitofrontal diameter (B), which can slow labour. The mentovertical diameter (A) presents in a brow presentation and is too large for vaginal delivery in most cases. The submentobregmatic diameter (C) presents in a face presentation, which can deliver if the chin is anterior.

questions.q: A woman with epilepsy who takes sodium valproate wants to become pregnant. What is the best advice?
options: Stop all antiepileptic drugs as soon as she conceives
Continue the same drug and dose, with no folic acid
Get a preconception review to switch to a safer drug, and take high-dose folic acid
Reduce the valproate gradually on her own once she is pregnant
questions.explanation: Valproate is linked to neural tube defects, other malformations and neurodevelopmental problems, so a specialist should review treatment before conception to consider a safer option (such as lamotrigine or levetiracetam) at the lowest effective dose. Abruptly stopping or self-adjusting drugs (A, D) risks seizures, which harm both mother and fetus. Folic acid in a higher dose is usually advised (B is wrong). Offer vitamin K to the newborn according to protocol, and encourage breastfeeding in most cases.

questions.q: By what age should a healthy, breastfed term baby regain birth weight?
options: 3 days
10–14 days
4 weeks
6 weeks
questions.explanation: Term babies lose up to 7–10% of birth weight in the first days, reach the lowest point on about day 3–4, and regain birth weight by 10–14 days. A baby who has lost more than 10%, or has not regained birth weight by 2 weeks, needs a feeding assessment (attachment, milk transfer, frequency) and evaluation for dehydration, infection or other problems.

questions.q: A multigravida at 6 cm has had no change in cervical dilatation for 3 hours. The fetal heart rate is normal and the mother is distressed. What is the most appropriate first step?
options: Arrange an immediate caesarean section without further assessment
Apply fundal pressure with each contraction to speed descent
Give ergometrine IM to strengthen the contractions
Assess power, passenger
questions.explanation: Slow progress needs a systematic assessment: contraction strength and frequency (power), fetal size, position and attitude (passenger), and the pelvis (passage), with a check for a full bladder, dehydration and exhaustion. Oxytocin is considered only when contractions are inadequate and there is no cephalopelvic disproportion or malposition. Immediate caesarean (A) is not justified without assessment. Fundal pressure (B) is unsafe. Ergometrine (C) causes tetanic contractions and is dangerous before delivery.

questions.q: A baby is in the left occipito-anterior (LOA) position. In which area of the mother's abdomen is the fetal heart best heard?
options: Left lower quadrant
Right lower quadrant
Left upper quadrant
Right upper quadrant
questions.explanation: In a cephalic presentation, the fetal heart is best heard through the baby's back and shoulder. In LOA, the back lies to the mother's left and anteriorly, so the heart is heard in the left lower quadrant, below the umbilicus. In right occipito-anterior (ROA) it is heard on the right (B). In a breech presentation the heart is usually heard above the umbilicus (C, D).

questions.q: When is the first routine HIV DNA PCR test done for an HIV-exposed infant under Kenya's PMTCT programme?
options: At birth only, for all infants
At 6 weeks of age, or at the first contact after that
At 9 months with the measles vaccine
At 18 months of age
questions.explanation: Early infant diagnosis uses a DNA PCR test at about 6 weeks, so that an infected baby can start ART early. Further virological tests follow the MoH schedule during the exposure period, and a final antibody test is done after breastfeeding has stopped. Birth testing is reserved for infants at high risk, not for all babies (A). Waiting until 9 or 18 months (C, D) delays treatment of infected infants.

questions.q: A woman at 30 weeks has preterm labour. If a tocolytic is used for a short time to allow antenatal corticosteroids to take effect, which drug is preferred?
options: Magnesium sulphate
Salbutamol infusion
Nifedipine orally
Diazepam
questions.explanation: WHO does not recommend tocolysis routinely, because it does not improve neonatal outcomes. Where it is used, nifedipine is the preferred agent for a short course of up to 48 hours, to allow steroids to work or to transfer the woman to a higher-level facility. Beta-agonists such as salbutamol (B) have more maternal side effects. Magnesium sulphate (A) is given for fetal neuroprotection before 32 weeks and for seizure prevention, not as a tocolytic. Diazepam (D) has no tocolytic role. Tocolysis is avoided with suspected infection, abruption, fetal distress or severe pre-eclampsia.

questions.q: In an area where hookworm is common, which deworming regimen is recommended for a pregnant woman?
options: Albendazole 400 mg daily for 3 days at 8 weeks
Ivermectin as a single dose at 12 weeks
Praziquantel 600 mg daily for a month
Albendazole 400 mg as a single dose in the second trimester
questions.explanation: In endemic areas, a single dose of albendazole 400 mg (or mebendazole 500 mg) is given after the first trimester, because hookworm contributes to maternal anaemia. Medicines are avoided in the first trimester when organogenesis occurs. Longer albendazole courses (A) are not routine, and ivermectin (B) and prolonged praziquantel (C) are not the standard regimens for this purpose. Deworming is part of anaemia prevention alongside iron and folic acid.

questions.q: Which findings suggest hypovolaemic shock in a woman with postpartum haemorrhage? Which combination is correct?
options: A, B, C
A, B, C, D, E
A, B, C, E
D, F
questions.explanation: Correct combination: A, B, C, E. The body compensates for blood loss with tachycardia and vasoconstriction, giving a fast, thready pulse and cool, pale, sweaty skin. Blood pressure falls late, urine output drops, and the woman becomes anxious, restless, then drowsy. Warm flushed skin with a slow pulse (D) and a bounding pulse with high BP (F) do not fit shock. Treat by calling for help, controlling the bleeding, raising the legs, giving oxygen, and starting two large-bore IV lines with fluids and blood.
