Advise her to switch to formula feeding from today onwards
Delay any review until the six-week postnatal clinic visit
questions.explanation: Weight loss greater than 10 % together with reduced urine output indicates inadequate intake and requires prompt assessment of feeding and infant well-being.

questions.q: A woman with a history of previous PPH is in the second stage. What is the most effective preventive measure for the third stage?
options: Delayed cord clamping only
Early cord traction without uterotonic
Physiological management
Active management with a uterotonic
questions.explanation: Women at higher risk of PPH benefit from active management of the third stage, including a uterotonic, to reduce blood loss.

questions.q: A woman at 32 weeks has blood pressure 160/105 mmHg, headache and visual disturbance. Proteinuria is present. What is the immediate priority?
options: Give oral antihypertensives alone and send her home to rest
Control BP, give magnesium sulphate and antenatal corticosteroids
Start outpatient monitoring and review her in one week's time
Do an immediate caesarean section without stabilising her first
questions.explanation: This is preeclampsia with severe features. Stabilisation with antihypertensives and magnesium sulphate, plus corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity, precedes decisions about delivery timing.

questions.q: A breastfeeding mother is prescribed a short course of ibuprofen for after-pains. What advice should she receive?
options: Wean the baby before starting the tablets
Continue breastfeeding, as ibuprofen is compatible
Take the drug only after the evening feed
Stop breastfeeding for 24 hours after each dose
questions.explanation: Ibuprofen is considered compatible with breastfeeding at standard analgesic doses.

questions.q: At 12 weeks a woman starts antenatal care. According to the WHO model adopted in Kenya, how many contacts are advised for a healthy pregnancy?
options: Twelve visits at monthly intervals
Four focused visits only
A minimum of eight contacts
Two visits, one per trimester
questions.explanation: WHO recommends at least eight contacts (12, 20, 26, 30, 34, 36, 38 and 40 weeks). Older NCK/focused ANC teaching used four visits; the current Kenyan guidelines use eight.

questions.q: A newborn is 4 hours old and has a blood glucose of 1.8 mmol/L (32 mg/dL). The infant is lethargic. What is the priority action?
options: Reassure the mother and review next morning
Offer a breastfeed and recheck in two hours
Give IV 10% dextrose and keep monitoring closely
Give oral sucrose only and observe
questions.explanation: Symptomatic hypoglycaemia requires urgent intravenous glucose treatment rather than feeding alone.

questions.q: A woman is 1 hour post-birth. Measured blood loss is 520 mL. Vital signs are stable. According to the 2025 WHO guidelines, what is indicated?
options: Immediate hysterectomy
Blood transfusion as first step
Observation only
First-response PPH treatment
questions.explanation: Measured blood loss ≥ 500 mL meets the threshold for initiating first-response treatment even if vital signs are still normal.

questions.q: A mother has had a caesarean section under spinal anaesthesia. When can breastfeeding usually be initiated?
options: After the spinal anaesthetic has completely worn off
As soon as mother and baby are stable, often in recovery
Only after 24 hours have passed following the operation
Only after she has taken her first oral fluids and meal
questions.explanation: Breastfeeding can begin as soon as the mother is alert and stable; spinal anaesthesia does not require a prolonged delay.

questions.q: During the newborn examination the midwife cannot elicit a red reflex in one eye. What is the appropriate action?
options: Recheck only at the six-week visit
Refer urgently for ophthalmology assessment
Document the finding and take no action
Reassure the parents that this is normal
questions.explanation: Absence of a red reflex may indicate cataract, retinoblastoma or other serious ocular pathology and requires urgent specialist referral.

questions.q: A midwife is caring for a woman in labour with confirmed ruptured membranes for 8 hours. What infection-prevention measure is most important?
options: Perform frequent vaginal examinations to monitor progress
Apply antibiotic cream to the perineum routinely
Limit vaginal examinations and maintain strict asepsis
Restrict all oral intake in labour
questions.explanation: Minimising vaginal examinations and using aseptic technique reduce the risk of ascending infection after membrane rupture.

questions.q: A stable preterm infant of 34 weeks is able to coordinate sucking. What is the preferred feeding method?
options: Continuous nasogastric tube feeding as the only method
Support breastfeeding or expressed breast milk feeding
Avoid any oral feeding until she reaches term age
Exclusive cup or bottle feeding with formula milk
questions.explanation: Breast-milk feeding, directly or expressed, is preferred for preterm infants because of its immunological and developmental benefits.

questions.q: A newborn is 1 hour old. Axillary temperature is 35.8 °C despite skin-to-skin contact. What is the priority action?
options: Rewarm actively under a radiant warmer and recheck regularly
Wrap him tightly in a cloth and leave him undisturbed
Give a warm bottle feed and then leave him undisturbed
Bathe him in warm water to raise his temperature quickly
questions.explanation: A temperature of 32.0–35.9 °C is moderate hypothermia and needs active rewarming with close observation.

questions.q: At the first antenatal visit a woman is found to have a positive syphilis test. What is the appropriate management?
options: Give no treatment because she has no symptoms
Treat promptly with benzathine penicillin
Delay treatment until the third trimester
Treat only if her partner tests positive
questions.explanation: Syphilis in pregnancy requires immediate treatment with penicillin to prevent congenital infection and adverse pregnancy outcomes.

questions.q: A mother is exclusively breastfeeding a 3-month-old infant and has not resumed menstruation. She asks about the Lactational Amenorrhoea Method (LAM). What is required for LAM to be effective?
options: Exclusive breastfeeding, amenorrhoea, baby under six months
Breastfeeding at night only with long gaps in the daytime
Any amount of breastfeeding, whether by day or by night
Breastfeeding with regular formula top-ups in between feeds
questions.explanation: LAM is effective only when all three criteria are met: exclusive breastfeeding, no return of menses, and infant younger than 6 months.

questions.q: A midwife is teaching perineal care after a second-degree tear. What is the most important advice?
options: Keep clean and dry, change pads often and use analgesia
Avoid washing the area at all during the first postnatal week
Sit in a bowl of salt water for several hours daily
Apply antiseptic cream to the stitched wound every hour
questions.explanation: Simple hygiene, frequent pad changes and pain relief promote healing and reduce infection risk.

questions.q: A woman at 34 weeks reports that fetal movements have been markedly reduced for 24 hours. What is the priority action?
options: Reassure her that movements normally decrease
Book a routine scan for the following week
Assess fetal well-being the same day
Advise her to wait another day
questions.explanation: A sustained reduction in fetal movements requires same-day evaluation of fetal well-being.

questions.q: A woman is bleeding after birth from an atonic uterus and tranexamic acid is to be given. What is the recommended dose?
options: 500 mg IV once, given as a rapid push over one minute only
1 g orally, with a second oral dose after three hours
1 g IV over 10 minutes; repeat once after 30 minutes if needed
2 g IV bolus repeated every hour until the bleeding stops
questions.explanation: WHO recommends tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 minutes as early as possible and within 3 hours of birth, with a second 1 g dose if bleeding continues after 30 minutes or restarts within 24 hours.

questions.q: On the WHO modified partograph used in Kenya, plotting of the active phase begins at which cervical dilatation?
options: 6 cm
5 cm
3 cm
4 cm
questions.explanation: The modified WHO partograph used in Kenya starts the active phase at 4 cm with alert and action lines. The 2018 WHO recommendations and the 2020 Labour Care Guide place the start of active labour at 5 cm. (Original key said 6 cm 'per WHO', which is incorrect.)

questions.q: A mother has deeply inverted nipples and is finding attachment difficult. What is the first-line approach?
options: Use a nipple shield for every feed from the first day
Advise her to stop breastfeeding altogether and use formula
Refer for surgical correction of the nipples before feeding
Skilled help with positioning and attachment techniques
questions.explanation: Most mothers with inverted nipples can breastfeed successfully with skilled help in positioning and attachment; devices are second-line.

questions.q: A mother who is fully breastfeeding asks when fertility is likely to return. What is the most accurate statement?
options: Fertility returns only after complete weaning
Fertility can return before the first menstrual period
Fertility never returns while she is breastfeeding
Fertility returns only after twelve months
questions.explanation: Ovulation can precede the first postpartum menses, so contraception is still needed if pregnancy is not desired.

questions.q: A woman with preeclampsia is discharged on day 5 with normal blood pressure. How long should blood-pressure monitoring continue?
options: No further monitoring is necessary
At least 1–2 weeks, with early review
Only if symptoms return at home
For 24 hours only after discharge
questions.explanation: Blood pressure can rise again in the first 1–2 weeks after birth; continued monitoring and early follow-up are recommended.

questions.q: A nulliparous woman has been having irregular contractions for 18 hours and is still 3 cm dilated. Maternal and fetal condition are good. What is the appropriate action?
options: Supportive care and reassessment
Start high-dose oxytocin
Artificial rupture of membranes at once
Immediate caesarean section
questions.explanation: Prolonged latent phase is managed supportively provided mother and fetus remain well; active intervention is not required solely on time.

questions.q: A newborn of 2 hours has a respiratory rate of 75 breaths/min, nasal flaring and intercostal recession. What is the priority action?
options: Refer for urgent medical evaluation
Encourage breastfeeding only
Delay any assessment for 2 more hours
Reassure that this is normal transitional breathing
questions.explanation: Tachypnoea with increased work of breathing is a danger sign and requires prompt assessment for respiratory or cardiac problems.

questions.q: On day 4 a woman’s lochia is pinkish-brown and moderate in amount. What does this indicate?
options: Retained products of conception in the uterus
Endometritis from an ascending uterine infection
Normal change from lochia rubra to serosa
Secondary postpartum haemorrhage in the early puerperium
questions.explanation: Lochia normally changes from red (rubra) to pinkish-brown (serosa) around days 4–10.

questions.q: A woman with severe hypertension in pregnancy needs urgent blood-pressure control. Which oral agent is commonly used as first-line in many guidelines?
options: Oral atenolol 100 mg daily
High-dose aspirin 300 mg
Oral nifedipine or IV labetalol
Magnesium sulphate on its own
questions.explanation: Nifedipine (short-acting oral), labetalol or hydralazine are first-line for severe hypertension in pregnancy; atenolol is avoided.

questions.q: A woman is day 3 postpartum with fever, uterine tenderness and foul-smelling lochia. After cultures are taken, what is the usual antibiotic approach?
options: Topical vaginal antibiotic pessaries inserted nightly
Oral amoxicillin for three days and then review at home
IV ampicillin, gentamicin and metronidazole until afebrile
Withhold all antibiotics until the culture results return
questions.explanation: Postpartum endometritis is treated with IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (WHO: ampicillin + gentamicin + metronidazole) until the woman is afebrile for 48 hours.

questions.q: A woman attends her first antenatal visit at 22 weeks. What is the most important action regarding the timing of care?
options: Start the recommended schedule of contacts from this visit
No further visits are needed unless she has complaints
Schedule her next visit only when she reaches 36 weeks
Tell her it is now too late for antenatal care to help
questions.explanation: Even if the first visit is late, the remaining antenatal contacts should still be provided according to the WHO eight-contact model.

questions.q: A midwife is considering artificial rupture of membranes to augment labour. Which condition must be excluded first?
options: Early labour with a vertex presentation
A maternal request for the procedure
Cord presentation or a high presenting part
Adequate regular uterine contractions
questions.explanation: Amniotomy is contraindicated when the presenting part is high or cord presentation is suspected because of the risk of cord prolapse.

questions.q: A term newborn has lost 9 % of birth weight by day 4 and is feeding well with adequate wet nappies. What is the appropriate action?
options: Continue breastfeeding support and recheck the weight soon
Readmit the baby for IV fluids and close monitoring
Start immediate formula supplementation after each feed
Stop breastfeeding and switch to cow's milk formula
questions.explanation: Weight loss of up to 10 % can be acceptable in a well, breastfed infant; close follow-up of feeding and weight is required.

questions.q: A woman is day 5 postpartum and asks about pelvic-floor exercises. When can she begin them?
options: After the lochia has stopped completely
Only if she has urinary incontinence symptoms
Only after the six-week postnatal check-up
As soon as comfortable, usually in the first days
questions.explanation: Gentle pelvic-floor exercises can begin early after birth once the woman is comfortable; they help recovery and reduce long-term problems.

questions.q: A woman received magnesium sulphate for eclampsia prophylaxis and delivered 6 hours ago. She is stable. When is the infusion usually discontinued?
options: After 48 hours of treatment
Immediately after the birth
About 24 hours after delivery
After 72 hours of treatment
questions.explanation: Magnesium sulphate is commonly continued for 24 hours after delivery (or after the last seizure) unless there are ongoing concerns.

questions.q: In the first 24–48 hours after birth, how often should a healthy newborn be breastfed?
options: Every 4–5 hours on a fixed schedule
Only when the mother feels her breasts are full
On demand, at least 8 times in 24 hours
Maximum 6 times per day
questions.explanation: Frequent, unrestricted breastfeeding (at least 8 times in 24 hours) supports milk production and prevents hypoglycaemia.

questions.q: Tocolysis is being used to allow completion of corticosteroids. What is the usual maximum duration of acute tocolysis?
options: 7 days
48 hours
14 days
Until 34 weeks
questions.explanation: Acute tocolysis is intended only to provide a short window (usually 48 hours) for corticosteroid administration and in-utero transfer; longer use is not beneficial.

questions.q: A woman in prolonged labour has a distended lower segment, a ridge between the upper and lower uterine segments rising towards the umbilicus, an oedematous vulva and scanty dark urine. What does this suggest?
options: Placental abruption with concealed bleeding
Obstructed labour with impending uterine rupture
Normal progress during the late first stage of labour
A full bladder from poor hydration only
questions.explanation: A pathological retraction (Bandl's) ring, an oedematous vulva and scanty concentrated urine indicate obstructed labour. Resuscitate, empty the bladder, give antibiotics and perform urgent caesarean section.

questions.q: A woman presents 48 hours after unprotected sex asking for emergency contraception. Which regimen is appropriate?
options: Misoprostol 800 µg orally as a single dose
Medroxyprogesterone 150 mg injection once
One combined pill daily for three days
Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg orally as a single dose
questions.explanation: Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg works best within 72 hours (some effect up to 120 hours). A copper IUD within 5 days is the most effective method.

questions.q: A woman at 24 weeks is newly diagnosed with HIV at antenatal care. What does Kenyan PMTCT policy advise?
options: Give ART only during labour and for six weeks after the birth
Start ART only if the CD4 count falls below 350 cells
Delay ART until after delivery to protect the fetus from exposure
Start lifelong ART the same day, with adherence counselling
questions.explanation: Kenya follows 'test and treat': all HIV-positive pregnant women start lifelong ART immediately (a dolutegravir-based regimen) with counselling and viral load follow-up.

questions.q: An HIV-exposed infant is born to a mother on ART. When should the first HIV DNA PCR test be done?
options: At 6 weeks of age, and at birth if high risk
At 12 weeks, using a rapid antibody test
At 6 months, together with a maternal CD4 count
At 18 months only, using a rapid antibody test
questions.explanation: Early infant diagnosis uses DNA PCR from 6 weeks (and at birth for high-risk infants). A final rapid antibody test is done at 18 months or after breastfeeding stops. Confirm schedule with the current NASCOP guideline.

questions.q: A baby is not breathing after drying and stimulation. Following Helping Babies Breathe, what must the midwife do within the 'golden minute'?
options: Clamp the cord and ventilate with a bag and mask within one minute
Suction the airway repeatedly for two full minutes first
Continue stimulating the baby for three more minutes before acting
Wait for the placenta to deliver before starting ventilation
questions.explanation: HBB aims to start effective bag-mask ventilation within one minute of birth in a baby who is not breathing; delay worsens outcomes.

questions.q: A stable woman at 10 weeks has an incomplete abortion with a uterus of 10 weeks size. Which method is preferred?
options: Observation at home for six weeks
Manual vacuum aspiration (MVA) of the uterus
Dilatation and curettage under general anaesthesia
Hysterectomy after full resuscitation
questions.explanation: WHO prefers vacuum aspiration (or misoprostol) over sharp curettage for evacuating the uterus. Offer post-abortion family planning and counselling.

questions.q: A woman is convulsing from eclampsia. What is the midwife's immediate priority?
options: Give oral fluids at once to prevent dehydration
Restrain her limbs firmly and insert a spatula between her teeth
Protect from injury, turn left lateral, clear the airway, give oxygen
Deliver the baby by vacuum before giving any drug
questions.explanation: Protect the airway and prevent injury, give oxygen, then magnesium sulphate. Restraint and objects in the mouth are harmful.

questions.q: A woman at 7 weeks of amenorrhoea collapses with severe lower abdominal pain and shoulder-tip pain. BP is 80/50 mmHg and pulse 128/min. What is the priority?
options: Reassure her and arrange an outpatient scan for next week
Resuscitate with IV fluids and prepare for emergency laparotomy
Give misoprostol and send her home with simple analgesia
Do a pelvic examination and wait for the symptoms to settle
questions.explanation: Shock with shoulder-tip pain after amenorrhoea is ruptured ectopic pregnancy until proved otherwise; resuscitate and operate urgently.

questions.q: A woman in labour has a frank breech presentation and the buttocks have descended to the perineum. What is the correct approach to delivery?
options: Keep hands off until the body is born to the umbilicus, then assist
Cut a large episiotomy and deliver the baby by firm traction
Pull firmly on the legs to speed up the delivery of the body
Apply fundal pressure at once to push out the trunk
questions.explanation: Breech birth is allowed to progress spontaneously ('hands off the breech'); traction can trap the head or extend the arms. Assist only when required, using the Løvset and Mauriceau–Smellie–Veit manoeuvres.

questions.q: A woman's last menstrual period began on 10 January 2026. By Naegele's rule, what is her expected date of delivery?
options: 17 October 2026
3 October 2026
24 October 2026
10 October 2026
questions.explanation: Add 7 days and subtract 3 months (or add 9 months), giving 17 October 2026. The rule assumes a regular 28-day cycle.

questions.q: At 28 weeks of pregnancy, what fundal height is expected?
options: About 24 cm, midway to the umbilicus
About 34 cm, near the xiphisternum
About 20 cm, at the level of the umbilicus
About 28 cm, within 2 cm either way
questions.explanation: From 24 weeks, fundal height in centimetres roughly equals gestational age in weeks (± 2 cm). The fundus reaches the umbilicus at about 20–22 weeks.

questions.q: A multiparous woman at 39 weeks delivers a vigorous term newborn. The midwife is preparing for the third stage. According to current WHO recommendations for prevention of postpartum haemorrhage, which uterotonic is preferred when a reliable cold chain cannot be guaranteed?
options: Misoprostol 600 µg orally as the routine first choice
Heat-stable carbetocin 100 µg IM
Ergometrine 0.2 mg IM given to all women
Oxytocin 10 IU IM stored at room temperature
questions.explanation: WHO recommends oxytocin 10 IU IM/IV as first-line prevention where quality-assured supply and a cold chain exist. Where oxytocin quality or cold-chain reliability is uncertain, heat-stable carbetocin is the preferred alternative. Oral misoprostol 600 µg is used when injectables are unavailable. Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension.

questions.q: At 6 hours after a normal vaginal birth the fundus is firm at the umbilicus and lochia is moderate. Her BP is now 148/96 mmHg (baseline 110/70) and she reports a frontal headache. What is the most appropriate next action?
options: Give an oral antihypertensive at once and discharge her home today
Reassure her that mild rises are normal and recheck BP the next day
Do a full pre-eclampsia assessment with urine protein and repeat BP readings
Encourage early ambulation and oral fluids, with review on day 7
questions.explanation: New-onset BP of 140/90 mmHg or more with a headache after birth needs prompt evaluation for postpartum pre-eclampsia, because eclampsia and stroke risk persist for days after delivery. (Original stem used 138/88, which is below the hypertension threshold.)

questions.q: A newborn born at 34 weeks is breathing poorly and has a heart rate of 90/min after drying and stimulation. Positive-pressure ventilation is started. What starting oxygen concentration is recommended?
options: 50% oxygen with titration only after five minutes
Room air only, whatever the saturation reading shows
100% oxygen until the heart rate exceeds 100/min
Low oxygen (21–30%), then titrate to SpO₂ targets
questions.explanation: Resuscitation of preterm babies starts with low oxygen (21–30%) and is titrated to pre-ductal SpO₂ targets; 100% oxygen is avoided at the start. Term/late-preterm babies (≥35 weeks) start at 21%. Check the exact gestational cut-offs against your edition of the AHA/AAP NRP.

questions.q: Eighteen hours after delivery a woman has severe perineal pain and cannot void. There is a tense, bulging, enlarging vulval haematoma. Her pulse has risen to 104/min and BP is 100/62 mmHg. What is the priority action?
options: Aspirate the haematoma with a needle and apply a firm perineal pad
Encourage her to void and reassess the pain after four hours of rest
Apply ice packs and give analgesia, then observe the swelling overnight
Prepare for incision, evacuation and ligation of bleeding vessels in theatre
questions.explanation: Small, stable haematomas are managed conservatively. An expanding, tense haematoma with urinary retention and a rising pulse needs resuscitation and surgical drainage with haemostasis.

questions.q: A newborn is 12 hours old. The midwife notes jaundice that is visible on the face and upper chest. The infant is breastfeeding well, has passed meconium, and has a normal temperature. Which action is most consistent with current neonatal jaundice guidelines?
options: Stop breastfeeding for 24 hours to lower the bilirubin load
Reassure her that jaundice in the first day is always physiological
Measure serum or transcutaneous bilirubin and plot it by age in hours
Start phototherapy at once without measuring any bilirubin level
questions.explanation: Jaundice appearing in the first 24 hours is always considered pathological until proven otherwise. Current practice requires prompt quantitative bilirubin measurement plotted on an hour-specific nomogram.

questions.q: A woman at 32 weeks gestation presents with painless vaginal bleeding. Ultrasound confirms placenta praevia. She is haemodynamically stable and the fetus is active. Which statement reflects current management priorities?
options: Do an immediate caesarean section whatever the gestational age or bleeding
Induce labour at 34 weeks to prevent any further episodes of bleeding
Allow bed rest at home with a weekly outpatient review of the bleeding
Admit for observation, give corticosteroids and plan caesarean at 36–37 weeks
questions.explanation: Stable placenta praevia is managed expectantly. A woman who has bled should be admitted; no vaginal examination is done. Steroids are given and caesarean is planned at 36–37 weeks.

questions.q: A term infant is born after prolonged rupture of membranes (18 hours). The infant is vigorous, has a normal temperature, and is breastfeeding. Maternal GBS status is unknown and she received no intrapartum antibiotics. What is the most appropriate observation plan?
options: Observe closely for 24–48 hours with regular vital signs before discharge
Give a single dose of IM penicillin to the baby and discharge early
Isolate the baby and perform a lumbar puncture as a routine procedure
Take a blood culture and start empirical IV antibiotics for the baby at once
questions.explanation: Rupture of membranes for 18 hours or more is a risk factor for early-onset sepsis. A well, vigorous term baby is observed closely; any sign of illness triggers a full sepsis work-up and antibiotics. GBS screening is not routine in Kenya.

questions.q: At the 6-week postnatal visit a mother reports low mood, poor sleep even when the baby sleeps, and feelings of worthlessness for three weeks. Her Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale score is 14. She denies thoughts of harming herself or the baby. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Advise her to stop breastfeeding to relieve her fatigue and poor sleep
Screen with EPDS, counsel supportively and refer for mental-health assessment
Reassure her that these are baby blues that will pass without treatment
Prescribe a sedative for sleep and review her again after one month
questions.explanation: Symptoms lasting beyond two weeks with worthlessness and an EPDS score above the cut-off indicate possible postnatal depression, needing counselling and prompt referral. (Merged with former Q97.)

questions.q: A nulliparous woman has pushed for 90 minutes. The head is at +2 station, contractions are weak (two in 10 minutes), the fetal heart rate is 140/min and there is no obstruction or descent in the last 30 minutes. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Continue passive pushing and wait without any intervention
Apply fundal pressure to hasten delivery of the head
Augment with oxytocin and reassess progress within 30–60 minutes
Proceed straight to caesarean section without augmentation
questions.explanation: Where second-stage delay is due to weak contractions and obstruction is excluded, oxytocin is appropriate. If contractions were adequate with no descent, instrumental birth or caesarean would be considered. (Original stem did not state that contractions were inadequate.)

questions.q: A multiparous woman is 8 cm dilated. The fetal heart rate shows repeated late decelerations that recover slowly. Maternal blood pressure is 150/95 mmHg. What is the priority action?
options: Continue labour as it is and reassess the fetal heart tracing again in 30 minutes
Turn her left lateral, give oxygen, stop oxytocin and call the obstetrician urgently
Give a tocolytic drug to reduce the contractions, then leave her to rest quietly
Rupture the membranes at once to speed up the delivery of the baby now
questions.explanation: Late decelerations indicate uteroplacental insufficiency. Immediate intrauterine resuscitation measures must be instituted while preparing for possible expedited delivery.

questions.q: A midwife is assessing a woman 2 hours after birth. Blood loss has been quantified at 320 mL using a calibrated drape. The woman’s pulse is 108 bpm and blood pressure is 95/58 mmHg. According to the 2025 WHO PPH guidelines, what does this situation indicate?
options: Immediate surgical intervention is required to control the bleeding
Criteria for initiating first-response PPH treatment have been met
Only IV fluid resuscitation is needed before any other treatment
Normal blood loss at this stage; continue routine observation only
questions.explanation: The 2025 WHO guidelines define the trigger for first-response treatment as measured blood loss ≥ 300 mL plus any abnormal vital sign (or ≥ 500 mL alone).

questions.q: A primigravida has been fully dilated for one hour. The head is still high at −1 station with marked caput and moulding (+++), contractions are strong (4 in 10 minutes), the fetal heart rate is normal and the urine is scanty and dark. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Suspect obstructed labour and arrange urgent caesarean section
Start a high-dose oxytocin infusion to improve the descent
Allow another two hours of pushing with continuous support
Apply fundal pressure while she pushes harder than before
questions.explanation: Strong contractions with a high head, severe moulding and no descent point to cephalopelvic obstruction. Oxytocin and fundal pressure risk uterine rupture. (Original stem described a normal second-stage delay but the key allowed more time.)

questions.q: A woman in the third stage has a sudden collapse, difficulty breathing, and a drop in blood pressure shortly after delivery of the baby. There is no excessive bleeding. What condition should the midwife consider first?
options: Amniotic fluid embolism
Postpartum haemorrhage
Eclamptic seizure
Simple vasovagal syncope
questions.explanation: Sudden cardiorespiratory collapse without significant bleeding in the immediate postpartum period raises suspicion of amniotic fluid embolism.

questions.q: A woman at 38 weeks has confirmed HIV infection and is in early labour. She has been on antiretroviral therapy with an undetectable viral load. What is the preferred mode of delivery according to current guidelines?
options: Instrumental delivery to shorten the second stage of labour
Vaginal birth, unless there is an obstetric indication for caesarean
Elective caesarean section for every HIV-positive woman in the facility
Induction of labour at 37 weeks regardless of her viral load
questions.explanation: When maternal viral load is undetectable on ART, vaginal birth is recommended provided there are no other obstetric indications for caesarean section.

questions.q: A woman in active labour has meconium-stained amniotic fluid. The fetal heart rate shows variable decelerations. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Proceed to an immediate emergency caesarean section for the meconium
Perform routine amnioinfusion to dilute the thick meconium in the liquor
Monitor the fetal heart continuously and prepare for newborn resuscitation
Augment labour with a high-dose oxytocin infusion to hasten delivery
questions.explanation: Meconium plus non-reassuring fetal heart rate patterns require continuous monitoring and readiness for neonatal resuscitation.

questions.q: A 29-week infant is receiving positive-pressure ventilation with 30% oxygen. At 3 minutes of life the pre-ductal SpO₂ is 62% (target 70–75%). What should the midwife do?
options: Increase the oxygen concentration stepwise and recheck SpO₂
Continue the same oxygen and recheck the saturation in 10 minutes
Reduce the oxygen to 21% to avoid hyperoxia in the preterm baby
Go straight to 100% oxygen and keep it running at that level
questions.explanation: Target pre-ductal SpO₂ rises with minutes of life: 60–65% at 1, 65–70% at 2, 70–75% at 3, 75–80% at 4, 80–85% at 5 and 85–95% at 10 minutes. Below target means increase oxygen stepwise; above target means wean. (Original gave 75% at 3 minutes, which is already in range.)

questions.q: A woman at 39 weeks has ruptured membranes for 12 hours, is not in labour, and is GBS-positive. She has not received antibiotics. What is the priority action?
options: Give IV antibiotic prophylaxis and plan prompt delivery by induction
Wait for spontaneous labour for another 12 hours, then reassess
Proceed to emergency caesarean without delay and without antibiotics
Induce with oxytocin alone and give no antibiotics to the mother
questions.explanation: Term rupture of membranes with known GBS colonisation needs intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis and timely induction. Routine GBS screening is not standard in Kenya, so this applies where results are available.

questions.q: A woman continues to bleed heavily after oxytocin, uterine massage and tranexamic acid. The uterus remains atonic. What is the next pharmacological step commonly recommended before surgical intervention?
options: Give high-dose IV antibiotics and continue to observe closely
Add a second-line uterotonic such as ergometrine or misoprostol
Give only IV fluids and wait for a response from the uterus
Go straight to hysterectomy without any further drug therapy
questions.explanation: When first-line oxytocin and tranexamic acid fail, additional uterotonics are used while preparing for mechanical or surgical measures. Hysterectomy is a last resort.

questions.q: A pregnant woman at 20 weeks has a haemoglobin of 9.8 g/dL. She is asymptomatic. According to current WHO recommendations, what is the appropriate action?
options: Give therapeutic iron with folic acid, treat malaria or hookworm, recheck Hb
Transfuse blood immediately because her Hb is below 10 g/dL today
Give no treatment until her haemoglobin has fallen below 7 g/dL
Continue prophylactic iron only and review her again at term
questions.explanation: Hb 7–9.9 g/dL is moderate anaemia, which needs a therapeutic iron dose (about 120 mg elemental iron daily) with folic acid, a search for malaria and hookworm (albendazole in the second trimester), and a repeat Hb in about 4 weeks. Transfusion is for severe or decompensated anaemia.

questions.q: An HIV-exposed newborn is born to a mother who was on effective antiretroviral therapy with an undetectable viral load. What is the usual infant antiretroviral prophylaxis recommendation?
options: Daily nevirapine from birth for at least 6 weeks, extended if high risk
No prophylaxis is needed because the maternal viral load is undetectable
Triple-drug ART for the first six months of life, then stop
Lifelong ART started for the baby within the first week of life
questions.explanation: Every HIV-exposed infant receives ARV prophylaxis. Kenya's regimen is daily nevirapine from birth (6 weeks for low risk; dual prophylaxis and longer duration for high-risk infants). Confirm duration with the current NASCOP guideline.

questions.q: A woman with preeclampsia is 48 hours postpartum. Her blood pressure remains 150/98 mmHg. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Restart magnesium sulphate infusion for a further 48 hours
Discharge her without any further blood pressure review
Continue BP monitoring and treat if the pressure stays raised
Stop all antihypertensive drugs immediately and recheck at six weeks
questions.explanation: Blood pressure can remain elevated or rise again in the days after birth. Continued monitoring and treatment are required.

questions.q: A woman at 30 weeks has confirmed preterm pre-labour rupture of membranes, no signs of infection and a normal fetal heart rate. Which pharmacological plan is recommended?
options: Immediate induction of labour with no steroids given before birth
Tocolytic drugs for seven days and no antibiotics at all
Antibiotics alone, with steroids only after 34 weeks of gestation
Corticosteroids and latency antibiotics such as erythromycin
questions.explanation: PPROM is managed with antenatal corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity and latency antibiotics to prolong pregnancy and reduce infection. Long-term tocolysis is not recommended. (Merged with former Q130.)

questions.q: A midwife is about to perform an episiotomy. What is the most important ethical and clinical requirement before proceeding?
options: Informed consent and a clear clinical indication
Ten minutes of crowning before cutting
Prophylactic antibiotics given before cutting
A routine plan for every first-time mother
questions.explanation: Episiotomy should never be routine. Informed consent is required, and the procedure is reserved for specific indications.

questions.q: A woman at 34 weeks with fetal growth restriction has reversed end-diastolic flow on umbilical artery Doppler. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Continue weekly outpatient monitoring and repeat the scan in a week
Start tocolysis and repeat the Doppler study in one week
Wait for term with twice-weekly CTG monitoring at home
Give corticosteroids and arrange delivery in a unit with neonatal care
questions.explanation: Reversed end-diastolic flow indicates severe placental insufficiency with a high risk of fetal death. At 34 weeks delivery is expedited in a facility able to care for a preterm baby, with steroids given if time permits.

questions.q: A woman is 90 minutes after birth. Measured blood loss using a calibrated drape is 450 mL. Pulse is 96 bpm and blood pressure is 108/68 mmHg. According to the 2025 WHO PPH guidelines, what is the correct action?
options: Begin first-response PPH treatment
Continue routine observation only
Give blood transfusion now
Prepare for immediate hysterectomy
questions.explanation: Treatment is indicated at ≥ 300 mL with abnormal vital signs or ≥ 500 mL alone. Neither threshold is met, so routine observation continues with ongoing quantification.

questions.q: A newborn requires resuscitation. Effective ventilation has been given for 30 seconds and the heart rate is now 70 bpm. What is the next action?
options: Give epinephrine through the umbilical vein at once without delay
Continue ventilation and reassess the heart rate after 30 seconds
Stop the resuscitation and observe the baby's colour for a minute
Start chest compressions straight away at a 3:1 ratio with oxygen
questions.explanation: Chest compressions begin only when the heart rate remains below 60 bpm after 30 seconds of effective ventilation. At 70 bpm, ventilation continues while the heart rate is reassessed.

questions.q: A breastfeeding mother is prescribed metronidazole for an infection. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Wean the baby permanently before the metronidazole is started
Stop breastfeeding for seven days after the last dose, then resume
Continue breastfeeding, since metronidazole is compatible
Use formula feeds only while she is taking the drug course
questions.explanation: Metronidazole is regarded as compatible with breastfeeding at standard doses. Temporary interruption is not routinely required.

questions.q: On the partograph the cervical dilatation has crossed the action line. Contractions are weak and the fetal heart rate is normal. What is the priority intervention?
options: Transfer her without any intervention or further assessment
Augment with oxytocin once obstruction has been excluded
Proceed to caesarean section without any trial of augmentation
Artificial rupture of membranes alone, with no other measures
questions.explanation: Crossing the action line with inadequate contractions indicates the need for augmentation once cephalopelvic disproportion or other obstruction has been ruled out.

questions.q: A woman in active labour has a temperature of 38.3 °C, foul-smelling liquor, and fetal tachycardia. What is the priority action?
options: Give oral antipyretics only and keep observing her progress
Start broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and prepare to expedite delivery
Delay the delivery until culture results become available
Do an immediate instrumental delivery regardless of dilatation
questions.explanation: These signs indicate chorioamnionitis. Intravenous antibiotics should be started promptly and delivery expedited according to obstetric assessment.

questions.q: A midwife is preparing for a high-risk delivery. Which action best ensures readiness for neonatal resuscitation?
options: Wait until after the birth before calling for any help
Rely on the mother's history alone to judge the risk
Prepare the oxygen cylinder only and no other equipment
Check equipment and call a skilled helper before the birth
questions.explanation: Anticipation and preparation, including equipment check and presence of a skilled helper, are essential components of the neonatal resuscitation chain of care.

questions.q: A woman with a twin pregnancy is at 28 weeks. What additional antenatal monitoring is commonly recommended compared with a singleton pregnancy?
options: No extra monitoring beyond the standard singleton schedule
Routine hospital admission from 24 weeks until delivery
More frequent growth scans and surveillance for complications
Weekly planning sessions for an elective caesarean birth
questions.explanation: Multiple pregnancies require increased surveillance for growth discordance, twin-to-twin transfusion and preterm birth risk.

questions.q: A woman in early labour requests non-pharmacological pain relief. Which method has the strongest evidence for reducing pain perception?
options: A mandatory supine position throughout the whole labour
Continuous support with mobility, water immersion and massage
Restricted oral fluids and food throughout early labour
Continuous electronic monitoring while she lies on a bed
questions.explanation: Continuous labour support and non-pharmacological methods (mobility, water immersion, massage) are associated with lower reported pain and reduced need for pharmacological analgesia.

questions.q: A woman is 12 days postpartum and develops sudden heavy bright-red bleeding with clots. The fundus is soft. What is the most likely cause?
options: A bleeding vaginal laceration from the birth only
Normal lochia with some clots on movement
Secondary PPH from retained products or infection
Primary PPH from uterine atony after delivery
questions.explanation: Secondary PPH is excessive bleeding from 24 hours up to 12 weeks after birth (WHO/RCOG), most often from retained tissue or infection. Some older NCK texts still say 6 weeks.

questions.q: A midwife is considering oxytocin augmentation. Which finding is a contraindication?
options: Inadequate contractions with a normal fetal heart rate
Signs of cephalopelvic disproportion or obstruction
Maternal exhaustion in spite of good contractions
Slow progress in a multiparous woman with a vertex
questions.explanation: Oxytocin must not be used when mechanical obstruction is present; it can cause uterine rupture.

questions.q: A newborn has had 20 minutes of effective ventilation, chest compressions and epinephrine with no detectable heart rate. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Discuss stopping resuscitation with the team and the parents
Continue indefinitely with the same resuscitation measures
Start a fluid bolus and wait for one hour before stopping
Give a double dose of epinephrine through the endotracheal tube
questions.explanation: The AHA/AAP NRP advises that stopping can be considered after about 20 minutes of complete and adequate resuscitation with no heart rate. Helping Babies Breathe, used at lower levels in Kenya, uses 10 minutes. (Original key cited 10 minutes under NRP.)

questions.q: A pregnant woman at 28 weeks has a haemoglobin of 8.9 g/dL despite taking iron supplements for 4 weeks. What is the appropriate next step?
options: Stop the iron tablets and wait until after the delivery
Transfuse blood at once regardless of her symptoms
Look for the underlying cause and consider parenteral iron
Increase the folic acid only and review her at term
questions.explanation: Persistent anaemia despite supplementation requires further investigation (e.g., compliance, malabsorption, or other causes) and possible parenteral iron or other therapy.

questions.q: A woman with gestational hypertension at 38 weeks has stable blood pressure on medication and no features of preeclampsia. What is the usual timing of delivery?
options: An immediate caesarean section today without trial of labour
Expectant management until she reaches 41 weeks of gestation
Induction only if proteinuria develops during the next weeks
Planned delivery from 37 weeks according to local protocol
questions.explanation: For gestational hypertension without severe features, delivery is usually planned from 37 weeks to balance maternal and fetal risks.

questions.q: A woman who is 4 weeks postpartum and fully breastfeeding wishes to have a copper intrauterine device inserted. What is the advice?
options: Only a hormonal IUD can be used while she breastfeeds
She must wait until her menses return after weaning
Insert the copper IUD if no contraindication exists
It is contraindicated until the baby is six months old
questions.explanation: Copper IUDs can be inserted from 4 weeks postpartum in breastfeeding women when infection and uterine involution have been assessed.

questions.q: A stable preterm infant is receiving Kangaroo Mother Care. How long should this method continue according to WHO guidance?
options: For the first 24 hours of life only, then incubator care
Until the baby has gained a weight of 2 kg in hospital
Only while the baby remains an inpatient in the hospital
Until about 40 weeks corrected age or until the baby resists it
questions.explanation: WHO recommends continued Kangaroo Mother Care for as long as the infant requires it, frequently until around term-equivalent age.

questions.q: A woman is 9 days postpartum and develops heavy bleeding with clots and a soft uterus. After initial resuscitation, what is the most important next investigation?
options: Reassurance that this is normal lochia for day nine
Immediate hysterectomy before any investigation
A routine blood culture as the only investigation
Ultrasound scan to look for retained products
questions.explanation: Secondary PPH is frequently caused by retained placental tissue; ultrasound helps confirm the diagnosis and guide further management.

questions.q: A non-vigorous term newborn is born. The umbilical cord is still intact. What is the current recommendation regarding cord management?
options: Clamp only after the placenta is delivered
Immediate clamping so resuscitation can start
Milk the cord toward the baby
Delay clamping for at least 60 seconds even if resuscitation is needed
questions.explanation: When the infant is non-vigorous and needs immediate resuscitation, the cord is clamped promptly so that effective ventilation can begin without delay.

questions.q: A woman with an uncomplicated dichorionic twin pregnancy reaches 37 weeks. What is the usual recommended timing of delivery?
options: Expectant management until 40 weeks
Immediate caesarean section at 36 weeks
Wait for spontaneous labour only
Induction or planned birth from 37 weeks
questions.explanation: Most guidelines recommend planned delivery of uncomplicated dichorionic twins from 37 weeks to reduce late-pregnancy risks.

questions.q: A nulliparous woman has been in the second stage for 3 hours with epidural analgesia. The fetal head is descending and the fetal heart rate is normal. What is the appropriate action?
options: Proceed to emergency caesarean section
Stop the epidural and continue
Allow more time with close monitoring
Do an immediate instrumental delivery
questions.explanation: Current guidelines permit a longer second stage in nulliparous women with epidural when progress continues and fetal condition is reassuring.

questions.q: A woman is in threatened preterm labour at 28 weeks. In addition to corticosteroids, what medication is given for fetal neuroprotection?
options: Progesterone only
Routine antibiotics
Long-term nifedipine
Magnesium sulphate
questions.explanation: A short course of magnesium sulphate is recommended before anticipated preterm birth (usually < 32 weeks) for fetal neuroprotection.

questions.q: A woman continues to bleed after uterotonics, tranexamic acid and bimanual compression. The uterus is atonic. What mechanical method is commonly used next?
options: Intrauterine balloon tamponade
Immediate hysterectomy
Routine packing of the vagina
High-dose antibiotics only
questions.explanation: Intrauterine balloon tamponade is an effective next step for refractory atonic PPH before resorting to more invasive surgery.

questions.q: A woman at 26 weeks has a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test result that meets criteria for gestational diabetes. What is the first-line management?
options: Plan an immediate delivery of the baby at 26 weeks
No treatment of any kind until the third trimester
Start insulin therapy immediately after the diagnosis
Dietary advice and self-monitoring of blood glucose
questions.explanation: Most women with gestational diabetes are managed initially with diet, exercise and self-monitoring of blood glucose; medication is added if targets are not met.

questions.q: A woman received a complete course of antenatal corticosteroids at 28 weeks. She is now 32 weeks and again at high risk of preterm birth within 7 days. What is the current advice on a repeat course?
options: Give weekly courses until she delivers
Give a full second course routinely
A single rescue course may be considered
Never repeat the course in any circumstance
questions.explanation: ACOG/RCOG allow one rescue course if birth is again imminent and the first course was 14 days or more earlier (as early as 7 days). WHO does not recommend routine repeat courses; use local protocol.

questions.q: During neonatal resuscitation the midwife needs to assess the heart rate quickly. What is the preferred initial method?
options: Palpating the umbilical cord only
Listening with a stethoscope over the chest
Using a pulse oximeter or ECG if available
Observing the chest wall alone
questions.explanation: Pulse oximetry or ECG provides the most accurate and continuous heart-rate assessment; auscultation is used when these are not immediately available.

questions.q: A maternal death occurs in a Kenyan health facility. According to the MPDSR guidelines, what is the first required step?
options: Notify the sub-county health office within 24 hours
Wait for the family to request an inquiry
Report it at the next quarterly review meeting
Notify the county only after one month has passed
questions.explanation: Kenya's MPDSR requires notification of every maternal death within 24 hours, followed by a facility review and a report to improve quality of care. Confirm timelines with the current MPDSR guideline.

questions.q: An Rh-negative mother delivers an Rh-positive baby and her indirect Coombs test is negative. What should be given?
options: Anti-D immunoglobulin 300 µg IM within 72 hours of birth
Anti-D immunoglobulin 50 µg IM after six weeks
Anti-D immunoglobulin 300 µg IM with no time limit
Anti-D immunoglobulin only if the baby is jaundiced
questions.explanation: Anti-D given within 72 hours prevents sensitisation and protects future pregnancies. It is not needed if the baby is Rh-negative.

questions.q: A woman 2 days after delivery has a temperature of 39 °C, pulse 124/min, respiratory rate 26/min, BP 86/50 mmHg and foul lochia. What is the priority in the first hour?
options: Take cultures, then start IV broad-spectrum antibiotics and fluids
Await culture results before starting any antibiotics
Give paracetamol for the fever and review again in four hours
Apply a warm compress and encourage early ambulation
questions.explanation: Suspected puerperal sepsis with shock needs antibiotics and fluid resuscitation within the first hour (the 'sepsis six'), with source control and senior review.
